speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON POLICY-ESTABLISHMENT OF INFORMATION CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 4 I tabled the report of the task force on information which had been asked to examine federal information services and to recommend ways in which the federal government might improve its communications with the Canadian people. I now propose to outline briefly the government's plans.
The task force made 17 major recommendations. We accept those recommendations in principle, with two exceptions. Recommendation number five proposed the establishment of a citizens advisory bureau and neighbourhood councils. The government is sympathetic toward this proposal but feels it warrants further study. Recommendation number ten suggested that a government agency undertake a role as public advocate which we feel more properly belongs to Parliament.
The task force found that the information responsibilities of the federal government have not been discharged effectively despite considerable expenditure. It was our suspicion of this which moved us to ask for this task force study in the first place. As a step toward rectifying this situation we have accepted a recommendation to set up a small new unit called Information Canada which will be established at the beginning of April as part of the Department of Supply and Services. The unit will report direct to a minister. I am asking the Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for York-Scar-borough, who is already responsible for citizenship, to take responsibility for its initial planning and development in order that it might be as ready as possible for operational status at the beginning of the new fiscal year.

This organization is proposed mainly for three reasons. First, Information Canada will promote co-operation among federal information offices now operating in mutual isolation. The object will be to increase effectiveness as well as to save money by reducing duplication in the use of staff and equipment and by better joint use of the government's information resources.
A similar approach was recommended by the Glassco Royal Commission on Government Organization. We expect that co-ordination will result in more coherent information, clearer and more understandable to Canadians than it has been in the past.
The second reason for establishing information Canada is that there are many information offices in the federal government, but each now speaks for its own particular departmental concern. There is no machinery to deal with information on broad governmental concerns affecting more than one department.
The third reason is to be able to learn better the views of the Canadian people. The unit is therefore designed not merely as a vehicle for dissemination of information but to provide better systems for Canadians to make known their viewpoints to their government.
I pause at this juncture, Mr. Speaker, to emphasize that the government recognizes the fact that the primary responsibility for conveying to the government the views and attitudes of Canadians has always remained and always should remain with Members of Parliament. The capabilities of the elected representatives in these respects should be strengthened and employed; in no sense is it the government's intention to diminish the proper role of the private member in representing the views of his constituents.
To achieve these three objectives we plan an organization whose new staff, exclusive of three component units being transferred from other government agencies, will total less than 150. Of this total, which will include administrative and clerical workers, most will come from the existing public service.

February 10, 1970
Information Canada
Information Canada will have about 25 information officers whose role will be to deal with information which is outside the normal concern of any single department and to assist the departments, on request, when supplementary resources are needed for particular occasions. The rest of the staff will be engaged in such tasks as answering public enquiries, co-ordinating existing departmental information work, advising on the application of modern technology to government information organizations, providing reports on public concerns, and developing efficient reference services both for pictures and the printed word.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)

The organization will be divided into four branches-one for planning and research; one to produce and distribute information; one to gather and publish information on the views of the public; and an administrative branch. The Exhibition Commission, the still photo library of the National Film Board, and the publishing and selling functions of the Queen's Printer will be transferred to Information Canada to be components of the production and distribution branch.
The net cost of the new organization, excluding amounts being subtracted from existing departmental information budgets, will be in the order of $1 million in 1970-71. When we add the current budgets of units being incorporated, the total budget will be about $7J million. Information Canada will be expected to achieve economies to offset part of its own costs after it has been extab-lished and operating for some time.
In summary, Information Canada is to be a small federal information unit along the lines of the task force's proposals. Every modern government maintains an information organization, many of them more centralized or larger than the one we contemplate for Canada. But their role is generally only to produce and distribute information. Information Canada will be equally concerned with what citizens wish to say to their government. Whatever they say through opinion surveys will be public information, subject, of course, to the protection of personal privacy, all reports on public viewpoints will be made public. I believe this material will be of substantial value to all members of this House in effectively representing the Canadian people.

We welcome the recommendation that information policy be referred to a committee of Parliament. I would go further than the task force and suggest that a parliamentary committee review not only the objectives, policies and operations of Information Canada but also the information objectives of all departments. This parliamentary scrutiny would, I think, be a healthy process, especially if the committee were to consider its role as not only a surveillance but also as the more positive task of proposing means to bring government even closer to the people.
That is the government's objective in making this announcement, and it will remain our objective as we pursue the difficult but essential task of expanding the dimensions of democratic dialogue in this nation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON POLICY-ESTABLISHMENT OF INFORMATION CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the announcement made by the Prime Minister is one of great importance. The cover design of the report of the task force which recommended the establishment of Information Canada bears an exclamation mark and a question mark. Perhaps the exclamation mark was intended to emphasize the far-reaching nature of the overhaul recommended and the question mark was intended to indicate the doubts about the recommendation that was being made.
There are several aspects of government information, of course. One of these relates to policy. The position taken by the white paper in Great Britain published in June, 1969, among others, was that the main responsibility for explaining policy to Parliament and to the public must continue to rest with the ministers.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON POLICY-ESTABLISHMENT OF INFORMATION CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON POLICY-ESTABLISHMENT OF INFORMATION CANADA
speechtext: This task force was not given any directions. In fact, I think it was told to keep away from the role of Parliament. Yet the task force nevertheless said, among other things, that the ministers must provide more informative answers in Parliament than has been the tradition.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON POLICY-ESTABLISHMENT OF INFORMATION CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON POLICY-ESTABLISHMENT OF INFORMATION CANADA
speechtext:
If I may say so, Sir, we see extraordinary evasion from day to day on the part of ministers opposite. In fact, it is almost the general rule rather than the exception for ministers to answer, not questions as posed to them, but other questions they would prefer
February 10. 1970

to have been asked. So, I suggest it is nonsense for this ministry to talk about setting up elaborate information services until the Prime Minister and his ministers are prepared to discharge their fundamental responsibility of answering questions in this chamber.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON POLICY-ESTABLISHMENT OF INFORMATION CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON POLICY-ESTABLISHMENT OF INFORMATION CANADA
speechtext:
I know there are differing views among members as to the wisdom of bringing the electronic media into this House, but it might very well have the advantage of compelling the ministers to give straightforward answers to questions that are placed before them.
The second aspect of information, of course, is that the services available to the citizen should be made known. What services are available, where they are available and how one obtains them should be known. It would seem obviously important that the citizens of the country have this information and that it be made available to them.
The task force recommended that the government assist the information services. I would have recommended that the government go further and assist existing community services that are strapped financially. It is extraordinary to me that this is one of the two recommendations made by the task force that the government has chosen not to implement. This recommendation directly relates to the knowledge the citizen has as to what services are available to him, yet it is not implemented. In spite of the impression given by the commentary of the Prime Minister, the establishment of this agency does not represent the implementation of the recommendations of the Glassco commission, which suggested a committee of co-ordination. It is a new superstructure being built within the government with regard to information services. The task force recognized at least some of the dangers inherent in the establishment of such an organization. It recognized that this could quite easily become a sort of ministry of propaganda. I say it is surely obvious that Information Canada could very easily become "manipulation Canada".

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON POLICY-ESTABLISHMENT OF INFORMATION CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON POLICY-ESTABLISHMENT OF INFORMATION CANADA
speechtext:
We must all be aware of that. The task force was sufficiently concerned with this problem that it recommended the establishment of rigid controls, but I do not find these controls when I read the report of the task force. It recommended the 21701-6
Information Canada
establishment of a parliamentary committee, but it has not been demonstrated yet in this chamber that a parliamentary committee has sufficient independent authority to really constitute a safeguard.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
The task force also recommended the appointment of a sort of public ombudsman relating to information. This is the second of the two recommendations the Prime Minister has chosen not to implement. So, speaking for myself and I think for members of the House generally in this respect, we want to see coordination of information services; we want to see the services administered efficiently. But we want to see this co-ordination without the establishment of another layer of bureaucracy with the distinct possibility of the manipulation of public opinion. It would be difficult to exaggerate this danger.
Information Canada is to gather information as well as disseminate or propagate it. I think it is significant psychologically that, while the task force spoke of this agency gathering information about the needs of the public, the Prime Minister in his statement spoke about it gathering information about the views of the public. I think this might have been a Freudian slip.
While the Prime Minister speaks about preserving the role of the Member of Parliament, it is difficult to envisage any way in which the role of the individual member of Parliament, as the person to be consulted about the views of the people is likely to be cut down more drastically than by this centralized information-gathering service which will feed information directly to the ministry.

This is carrying the regional desks of the government much further. My hon. friends opposite will become mere ciphers and members on this side of the House will not be the only "nobodies" after this.

Information Canada

speechtext: Hear, hear.

This is a dangerous proposal. It should not be proceeded with now. This step should not be taken now, particularly in view of the obvious concentration of authority in the government as opposed to this House and, if I may say so, in the Prime Minister as opposed to the members of his government.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON POLICY-ESTABLISHMENT OF INFORMATION CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON POLICY-ESTABLISHMENT OF INFORMATION CANADA

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON POLICY-ESTABLISHMENT OF INFORMATION CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I found the Prime Minister's statement a very disturbing one, both because of what it said and because of what it failed to say. It failed to tell us what information the Prime Minister is speaking about. Are we talking about providing information to the people of Canada and explaining to them the government policies, which is perfectly necessary and desirable, or are we talking about, as I suspect from the statement we have just heard, an agency to control and manage the news the Canadian people will obtain from the government? I cannot help feeling that the super organization, the establishment of which has just been announced, is mainly for the purpose of managing the news emanating from the government and, if I may put it this way, that the agency will operate as a perpetual election campaign for the party in power.
The Prime Minister said that he welcomes the establishment of a parliamentary committee to review the objectives, policies and operations of Information Canada and, not only that, but to review the policies in the various departments. I say to the Prime Minister that if this is a genuine desire, then a

parliamentary committee should have been set up to discuss the objectives, policies and operations of Information Canada before that agency was formed. Before the Prime Minister made his announcement, the people who have studied this matter and have presented the plan to the government should have appeared before a committee of this House. We should have been given the opportunity to ask them questions to find out exactly what this agency is going to do. The failure of the government to bring it before a committee of the House, and the fact that it has presented us with a fait accompli, is precisely one of the things that makes me unhappy and suspicious of the purpose of this super organization.
No one denies that there is a need, as the Glassco report indicated, for co-ordinating the information services of the government. God alone knows that many of them are inefficient and much can be done to improve them. No one denies the need for getting rid of the duplication of staff and equipment that is now to be found in various departments of the government in connection with information services. But there is nothing in this statement that suggests there will be any reduction in the approximately $200 million now being spent on information services by the departments, only a suggestion that another $1 million will be added to what is now being spent on a super agency of the sort described.
The Prime Minister makes a great deal of the need to give the people of Canada information and to find out what they think. Permit me to say a word about each of those things. We have given him an opportunity to do that in this House. We took the government at its word that it really meant it when it said that it was in favour of full disclosure of government policies and government thinking. So, we have asked questions during the oral question period; we have placed questions on the Order Paper, and we have placed numerous motions for the production of various papers on the Order Paper of this House. When the government has asked for the production of a study made in order to assist the government to arrive at a policy, almost every time the government has refused to produce those study papers. I say to the Prime Minister that he has had the opportunity to prove to the members of the House and to the people of Canada that this government really means what it says when it talks about full disclosure of information to the people of this country and that he has failed to take advantage of that opportunity.
February 10, 1970

On the contrary, the government has refused to give the information to which members of this House are entitled and to which the people of Canada are entitled.
I cannot support the proposal of the Prime Minister until, in dealing with oral questions, written questions, and motions for the production of papers of various sorts, the government shows its good faith and its firm intention to inform the people of Canada. This it has not done until now.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
What does the Prime Minister say when he speaks about expanding the dimensions of democratic dialogue in this nation? This is the last phrase in his statement, the peroration, and a fine-sounding mouthful. But what in fact is he proposing? He is proposing a super agency to carry on a Gallup poll in this country. Who will compose the questions that the people of Canada will be asked? And what bias will there be in the questions that are thus composed? How do you find out what the people of Canada want and think- by giving them pre-arranged and premanaged questions to answer? Sure, you will get the answers you want, and that I suggest is precisely what the government wants this super agency to do, to get the answers it wants from the Canadian people.
The way you should find out from the ordinary people what they want, what they need, what hurts them, what they are looking for and what their aspirations are is for Members of Parliament to meet with them in their constituencies, and to listen to them, rather than by asking them pre-arranged questions and getting predetermined answers.
So, Mr. Speaker, in my view and in the view of my colleagues the proposal for Information Canada is another regrettable sham in the alleged participatory democracy about which the Prime Minister, in particular, and other members of his party talk. It is utterly regrettable that we should have before us another super agency, costing more money, doing nothing that is not already being done, except acting as an agency for controlling and managing the news that is to come out of the government. The only purpose is to befuddle, deceive and mislead the people; it is not to inform them.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON POLICY-ESTABLISHMENT OF INFORMATION CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have carefully listened to the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to the effect that the task force 21701-6i
Information Canada
made 17 important recommendations which the government accepts in principle, with two exceptions.
The Prime Minister went on to say:
The task force found that the information responsibilities of federal governments have not been discharged effectively despite considerable expenditure.
Mr. Speaker, if the government is short of information it has only itself to blame. I think that, as one can read in a paragraph of his statement, the federal members of Parliament, whatever their political affiliation, convey information to the government. However, as was mentioned earlier by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), we are getting from the Prime Minister and the other members of the Cabinet arrogant answers to our questions although they are of general interest. They do not have the courage to give reasonable replies.
That is the first finding the task force should have reached in its study. As a matter of fact, if the government refuses to give us sensible answers, what will be the use of information services? They will be used mainly to find jobs for friends of the government, party stalwarts, and for political scheming.
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister also said:
A similar approach was recommended by the Glassco Royal Commission on Government Organization. We expect that co-ordination will result in more coherent information, clearer and more understandable to Canadians than it has in the past.
The machinery does exist, even though the Prime Minister stated:
There is no machinery to deal with information on broad governmental concerns affecting more than one department.
Mr. Speaker, we have an information agency that costs us a fortune, the CBC, which, instead of keeping the government aware of public opinion, or the public aware of government action, spends some $186 million yearly to support tourists who are traipsing in Viet Nam, Belgium, Biafra and Nigeria. The CBC forgets to tell us what is going on in Canada, yet so-called officials generously paid by the Canadian people travel around the world.
Mr. Speaker, the CBC radio network should devote one hour a week to report on the activities of Parliament so that the public will know what is happening in Ottawa. But no, sir! Every two or three months, we are allowed six minutes and fifty seconds on The Nation's Business in order to keep people

February 10, 1970
Farm Machinery
Informed, while three quarters of the news heard on The National deal with foreign subjects. This is how they forget to tell the Canadian people what is going on in their own country.
Mr. Speaker, we should use the media available to us. Each week, the CBC should put aside one hour's broadcasting time and divide it equally among the four federal political parties. We could then inform the people of what goes on in the House and we might even grant to the public an additional hour of broadcasting time to enlighten Parliament on public opinion. But the government is taking no steps in that direction. We are ill informed by the government's fault and Information Canada will not remedy the situation if we continue with the same methods.
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister said:
-the primary responsibility for conveying to the government the views and attitudes of Canadians has always remained and always should remain with members of Parliament.
If it remains with Parliament, let us start by respecting the members of Parliament who have representations and suggestions to offer the government.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that Information Canada will become a propaganda agency for the government, and this offers some danger. Organizations like the CBC should serve to inform the public and the government.
A few minutes ago, I suggested that one hour per week be put at the disposal of the political parties and not 6 minutes and 50 seconds every two months, whereas one hour is allotted to Robert Charlebois, who keeps cursing while he is on. Since all kinds of European socialists and communists are invited as guests on CBC programs, should not this federal agency serve the needs of the people who pay its operation costs?
Let us ask the CBC to respect not only the government but also the Canadian parliament, which actually represents the population. That organization could work as a link between the public, that is the people we represent, and the duties we have assumed towards them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will try to be as brief as possible. With regard to the stern section of the vessel, which, as I explained yesterday, is still afloat, there is now an effort under way to get it more buoyant so it will be possible to tow. As is the case now, with so much oil-I am not sure if this is a contradiction in terms-in the forward part of the stern, it is not possible to tow it. In so far as the forward section is concerned, there is no chance whatever of salvage in the sense of moving it off the rock.
A controlled experiment was conducted yesterday with burning. This was with the use of glass pellets and benzine and also using magnesium flares and divers to get the whole business alight. This has proved successful and it is now our intention to proceed with this but letting the oil out in controlled quantities for burning so that the conflagration will not at any time be so great that the smoke problem might constitute a pollution hazard of another kind. Mr. Speaker, before we have the vote on third reading, I should like to say a few words. It is very difficult to be highly critical of Bill C-136 because it is a great step forward in respect of the expropriation laws of Canada. When
February 10, 1970

we realize that the last time a major amendment was made to this act was in 1886, the necessity for amendments becomes evident and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) should be congratulated for bringing this bill forward. During the debate on the report stage, the minister brought forth a motion in respect of clause 14(3) of the bill. Unfortunately, because of illness and another appointment, I was unable to be here. In his remarks the minister mentioned this was the first time since he had been Minister of Justice that he had failed to accept at the report stage a decision of the committee. He also suggested there might have been some rather peculiar things happening in the committee, and that we almost used a shotgun to bring forward the amendment before the committee. He said he was not casting any reflection on any member but suggested that, on sober reflection, probably members would agree with him.
It was I who brought forward the amendment to this clause in the committee. I am sure the minister and you, Mr. Speaker, would like to hear the reason I brought forward the amendment, because it is a matter of great importance. I believe my experience in expropriation matters, and that of many other members, has been much the same. When it comes to expropriation, we find that the Crown or the expropriating authority is in the superior position at times and can play a cat and mouse game with the person whose property is being expropriated. The Crown has always held the strong position of having most of the competent appraisers in the country on its side in matters of expropriation. The Crown also often has the good fortune of having some of the best counsel plead its case. This places the expropriated owner in a very difficult position in respect of bargaining effectively with the expropriating authority.
I brought forward an amendment which said, in effect, that the expropriating authority would give the expropriated owner not only a copy of the appraisal on which the compensation was based, but also a copy of all appraisals because it seemed to me the whole philosophy behind expropriation is that the person should be entitled to full and fair compensation for the expropriated property. If given all the appraisals within the control of the expropriating authority the person concerned, along with his real estate agent, appraiser or lawyer could determine whether an offer was fair and reasonable and whether he was receiving full and fair compensation. I
Expropriation
was quite surprised, after making my remarks on the amendment, that 75 per cent of the members of the committee voted for the amendment. This created quite a shock for the Minister of Justice and his officials. They immediately set about correcting the situation. As the minister said, this is the first time he has failed to accept an amendment brought forward at the committee stage by any member.
In his remarks yesterday the minister set forth some of the possible consequences of allowing the amendment to remain in the form in which it appeared at the committee stage. I was really amazed to hear him say the department might have to resort to subterfuge by obtaining only oral appraisals in respect of expropriation matters. I have heard it said that in matters of law, the Crown never wins and never loses. Surely, there is an onus on the Crown or on the expropriating authority not to allow itself to be placed in a position where it feels it is winning or losing. I believe its position at all times should be that the offer it presents to the owner whose property is being expropriated is a just and fair offer. The suggestion that the government would resort to subterfuge and obtain oral appraisals in order to outsmart the person whose property is being expropriated is not in keeping with the philosophy of government.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
He also suggested a problem might be created by having only one appraisal. I think it should be brought to the attention of the House that in Ontario, when a matter goes to arbitration, ten days before the hearing the parties must exchange the appraisals that they have obtained, either on behalf of the expropriating authority or on behalf of the owner of the expropriated land. I should like to see the able Minister of Justice suggest that if the case does go to arbitration we at least keep in line with the Ontario law by making it a rule that all sides exchange the valuations they have obtained on the expropriated property. This would be in keeping with the spirit of fairness to the owner whose land is expropriated. Here, I am not referring to the person who has a large tract of land, who can bring in the best appraisers and legal counsel to speak on his behalf, but to the ordinary person whose land is expropriated for some public purpose and who does not have legal counsel or appraisers at hand.

speechtext: The House resumed from Wednesday, February 4, consideration of the motion of Mr. Chretien that Bill C-152, to amend the National Parks Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITION, ACQUISITION, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few moments during which I participated in the debate on this bill, I suggested that it had been on ice for a long time but I felt that as it thawed it would be revealed as a fishy proposition. As a matter of fact, all of us know that fishy products tend to be slightly odoriferous. I would like to underline what I said on the earlier occasion by saying that if you take a piece of rather stale fish and freeze it, it is still stale when it is thawed.
In any event, I think that my remarks are justified because those of us who have been involved in the situation surrounding the introduction of this bill realize full well there is much more here than meets the eye in the legislation. I think probably the most important amendment in principle to the National Parks Act for some time is to be found in clause 13 which reads as follows:
There is hereby established a corporation for the purposes set forth in this Part, to be known as the National Parks Leaseholds Corporation.
Perhaps it is worthwhile reminding the House at this stage of the circumstances in which we were first made aware of this proposal. The Standing Committee on Northern Affairs had made a tour of the Banff and Jasper parks, had heard an extensive series of briefs from people interested in park matters, and also briefs outlining the problems of

the residents of those two communities. We had returned to Ottawa and had held further meetings here. The committee was at the point of preparing its report for presentation to the House when the then minister of Indian affairs and northern development appeared before the committee on March 14, 1967 and made a statement to us in which cursory reference was made to the hearings and the evidence before the committee. I should like to quote from page 2 of the press release containing the statement by the minister. It reads:
I would like to announce now, to recommend to parliament the enactment of legislation to establish a National Parks Leasehold Corporation for the purpose of administering these leases. This corporation will be independent, subject only to its statute, and any written directions of the minister.
A little further on, it reads:
By this measure we intend that commercial leases will be administered on commercial principles and on these principles only-
Then, it continues:
We would also of course expect that operating on sound commercial principles the corporation would, firstly, secure the necessary volume of investment for the visitor facilities needed and, secondly, ensure that the return to the taxpayers as a whole from these commercial concessions was adequate, which I do not think is the case today.
I recognize that the statement made by the then minister could be the subject of a great deal of debate. But from my point of view the introduction of part III of the National Parks Act can best be summed up by stating that it represents a form of creeping commercialism into the national parks administration of Canada. I think the discussions that took place before the committee earlier revealed quite clearly that that will be the result of the passage of this legislation. I contend that this is basically contrary to the spirit of the national parks trust, and it is not something which should be supported by this House.
The argument that this corporation will be independent of the minister may, on the face of it, have its attraction to some people. I suggest to you, however, that what it means is that once we set up a commercial corporation to be operated on commercial principles, one that is independent of the minister, we are paving the way for the inroads of commercialism into the national parks of Canada on a scale that we have not seen before. I submit that this is not something to which those who believe in the value of the parks as part of the national parks trust should lend their support. What we are in effect doing by this proposal is to set aside certain enclaves
February 10, 1970

within the parks free from the control of the parks people.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
In other words, we are saying to the people to whom we entrust the administration of the parks, "No longer will certain parts of the parks be under your administration. We are going to turn over certain parts of the national parks to people whose philosophy is commercialism." The result is that the parks people who are concerned with parks as parks, whether they be ecologists or naturalists, will no longer have any direct say in the activities that take place in certain parts of the parks. This is why I suggest we should oppose what I call creeping commercialism within the national parks system in Canada, and on that ground we should refuse to lend our support to this bill.
Secondly, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that by this bill we are creating an unnecessary and double bureaucracy. We already have a national parks administration. Now, we are proposing to set up new machinery which will function outside the parks branch. We are to have a new corporation with presidents, directors, staff and all the rest of it to do a job that I suggest can be done quite well by competent administrators in the department, whether employed in the local park areas, in the regional park areas, or in the national headquarters at Ottawa, and who would operate the parks within the spirit of the national parks trust. In effect, we will be saddling the administration of the national parks with an unnecessary bureaucracy and that, I submit, is a second ground for opposing passage of the bill.
There exists a myth in some people's minds that people who are employed directly in the public service for a salary are somehow incompetent individuals! I would not say that there have never been incompetent individuals employed in the public service, but by and large I submit that concept is a myth. I do not believe it is necessary to set up all of the political bureaucratic machinery of an independent corporation, separate from the normal operations of the department, in order to look after certain small parts of the national parks that have been leased to individuals. So, Mr. Speaker, I oppose this bill because I believe it will result in the creation of what I have referred to as a double bureaucracy.
But, Mr. Speaker, there are other ancillary reasons why we should oppose this piece of
National Parks Act
legislation, and particularly oppose its passage at this time. I submit that anyone who participated in the hearings of the committee in 1967 cannot help but agree that, in effect, the introduction of this legislation is a cover-up for the refusal of the administration to face up to certain situations in a realistic manner. Mr. Speaker, I suggest you cannot cure a cancer with a poultice, and so far as I am concerned this legislation is simply an attempt to wrap a poultice around a situation in the national parks administration. This proposal is not one that warrants the support of this House at this time.
The members of the committee who visited Banff and Jasper-I refer to Banff and Jasper in particular because I think it is primarily out of the situation in Banff and Jasper, and to a lesser degree in Waterton, that this legislation has been developed-cannot help but agree that the citizens of those two communities came before that committee in good faith. They felt this was a real opportunity for them to be heard before the highest court in the land, and that they were entitled to a fair hearing.
It has been a matter of considerable grief to me ever since that time that the committee report, which was never debated, simply amounted to a complete whitewash of the strongest objections of the citizens of Banff and Jasper with respect to certain aspects of the administration of parks policy which related to their communities. I felt ashamed that the committee, in dealing with the matter of leases, took the attitude that, rather than have a committee of Parliament recommend that the viewpoint of these citizens be dealt with in equity by Parliament, any differences of opinion on leasing matters should be left to the courts to test the validity of the citizens' cases. The reference was particularly to the question of the perpetual leases that had been issued within the parks boundaries in earlier years.
When I made reference to this subject during the discussion of Parks estimates in the House on June 9, 1967, the first opportunity that there was to discuss the question in the House, I made it quite clear I felt a mistake had been made in the issuing of these perpetual leases. I felt that parliament should come to grips with the situation. If I may, I would just quote what I had to say as recorded at page 1360 of Hansard of that date:
I want to state my view quite clearly. I do not believe that these perpetual leases should be allowed to continue forever. I am not learned in the law, but it appears to me that the way in which

February 10, 1970
National Parks Act
some of these leases were drafted comes pretty close to being the equivalent of title in fee simple as we ordinarily understand it in other parts of the country outside of park boundaries.
I went on to suggest that we should in effect, approach this matter in the spirit of what would normally be considered to be an expropriation proceeding. Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, it is rather ironic that we should be discussing this matter when the House has just given third reading to a bill dealing with procedures of federal expropriation, which one of my colleagues referred to as having brought the matter of expropriation into the 20th century. It is ironic that we should now be dealing with a proposal relating to leases in the parks, and in particular the perpetual leases, which will leave those leases forever within the ambit of the concepts of the 19th century. This, so far as I am concerned, is a third ground for opposing the passage of the bill.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The fourth reason why I think we should oppose this bill, and in particular in the context of the current situation, is somewhat related to the third. It relates particularly to Banff and Jasper and the question of perpetual leases. The fourth reason is that if this bill is passed it will perpetuate, as long it remains on the statute books, the existing colonialism in the towns of Banff and Jasper. They will become to an even greater degree than they are now, company towns. At least now, the citizens in those communities have some form of appeal directly up through the political process which we pride ourselves is a democratic one in Canada. But, Mr. Speaker, once the property within the townsites of Banff and Jasper is put in the hands of this corporation, as I understand it this corporation will be the end-all and the be-all of law so far as property holding in Banff and Jasper is concerned, and that is a situation which I say is simply not good enough. I have made it clear before and I make it clear again that I do not believe private property should be held within the parks; that property, if it is going to be used by individuals, must be held under some form of lease.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that in this Parliament long ago we should have come to grips with the question and should have dealt with it in the manner the people of Banff and Jasper asked us to deal with it, that is, in Parliament. Having done that, we would have paved the way to take the step that I suggested in this House on June 9, 1967. On that

occasion, I suggested that we pass legislation granting to Banff and Jasper the status of towns under special federal charter so that they might have dealings in a normal way under agreement between the federal and provincial governments for the municipal services available to other communities in the province of Alberta. It is because these towns are within the parks that there would have to be special charters. I suggested then that there are anomalies within the parks, but there they are and we must recognize the fact. The people living in those communities are citizens of Canada and should have the same rights as other citizens for democratic self-employment in their own communities which they do not have now. Had Parliament taken the step at that time, there would now be some local authority with rights under the law to deal with an agency such as this, if it is to be set up as custodian of land within the boundaries of the communities.
As I understand it, Mr. Speaker, the proposal before us would make the people of Banff and Jasper forever the prisoners of this corporation. Many of the people who have grown up in the province from which I come know what is meant by the term "company town". I suggest that in the 20th century the Parliament of Canada should not be moving to create company towns anywhere in this country, but rather in the reverse direction. The proposal to add this provision under the National Parks Act will, in my view, do exactly that as far as the communities of Banff and Jasper are concerned. That, Mr. Speaker, is the fourth reason why I feel that I cannot support the bill.
As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, and as far as my party is concerned, we do not want to become involved in the kind of argument that has gone on in this chamber and in committee as to which administration was responsible for what in respect of leasing policies.

Read the lease, beginning at clause 16, where it says the lease shall terminate if the lessee fails to perform, observe or keep any of the covenants and agreements herein contained, or violates any of the provisions of the National Parks Act or regulations issued pursuant thereto. There is no provision for compensation in such an event. Who interprets the lease? It is the corporation which will interpret the lease. Who says that the lessee has made a mistake? It is not a court of law. It is the corporation or the minister. It is one of these authorities which will say: You have violated these laws, so you are out.
The tenant may reply: I do not intend to get out; I shall go to law. But it takes a long time to go to law when the Department of

As I have just mentioned, a tenant can be thrown out on the grounds that he has broken a park regulation. Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to take part in this debate and to follow the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), who was the former federal representative for a portion of Rocky Mountain riding and had the privilege of representing Banff National Park in this House for many years. I have a number of reservations about this bill and the rapid passage of the bill through the House. It is a bill that is of greatest importance to my riding. Its impact on Banff, Jasper and Waterton will be greater than on any other community in the country.
It was disappointing for me to hear the previous speaker fail to seize upon the real and crucial problems that exist in our national parks, and particularly those in Rocky Mountain riding. In the speeches that I have heard up to this point there has been an attempt to suggest that the introduction and passage of this bill through the House is strictly a political maneouvre. I suggest this is simply an evasion of the real problem.

February 10, 1970
National Parks Act
In the national parks of Canada, and particularly in Banff, Jasper and to a lesser extent Waterton, a very serious situation has been created among those communities that are permanent. People living in those communities do not have the same democratic privileges and rights possessed by Canadians living outside our national parks. They have no local government. In addition, since the property is federal property, the local member of the provincial legislature has very little authority or jurisdiction with regard to them. As a result, virtually the only elected representatives to represent the people of the townsites and communities in our national parks are the local members of Parliament, whoever they may be at any given time.
This situation has resulted in a complete lack of communication between those governed and those governing. It is different from the situation that obtains in other communities where there is dialogue and communication between the elected municipal officials and the electors, between the provincial legislature members and the electors, and between the federal members of Parliament and the electors.
I believe the key issue here is that of communication, and that of the community accepting responsibility for its own welfare. This lack of communication is not something that has arisen within the last year and a half or even within the last 6, 7 or 10 years. It has been a characteristic of the communities of Banff and Jasper almost since their inception.
A number of studies and reports have been made about Banff and Jasper in order to determine by what method these communities should be administered. I want to emphasize the word "community", because all too often those of us who live outside our national parks, particularly outside Banff and Jasper, think these communities are populated by businessmen. This is far from the fact.
For example, Jasper is populated largely by employees of the Canadian National Railways. The first railway went through Jasper in 1911 or 1912, and ever since that time this community has been a divisional point for one of our trans-continental railways. So, it is easy to see that the largest single group populating Jasper consists of employees of the Canadian National Railways, not businessmen. I am sure we would find that those with investments in businesses in Banff and Jasper account for less than 10 per cent of the population in those towns.
[Mr. Sulatycky.l
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
We have been very slow to recognize this and we think of these communities as comprising wealthy people from Calgary, Edmonton and other cities and towns who have summer cottages in our national parks. I quite agree that it is not proper to allow the existence of summer cottages in national parks. It is quite a different thing to have people who must reside there because of their employment or occupation in order to serve the millions of Canadians and others we encourage to visit these parks. These people must reside there in order to serve the tourists, the railways, the highways, the lines of communication and the pipelines which traverse these national parks. We must recognize that these are communities similar to communities outside the national parks. Unfortunately, our predecessors in Parliament for many years have failed to recognize this. The department which has been responsible for the administration of the townsites of Banff, Jasper and Waterton have failed to recognize this fact.
The people living in these towns have been administered from Ottawa with no say in their own affairs or in the administration of their own townsites. This gulf between the administrators and the administered continues to increase year after year. There is now a greater degree of antagonism. The administrators are antagonistic toward the residents of the park. They refer to them as businessmen and cover up the facts in this way. They are not businessmen. There is a natural human reaction on the part of these people who reside in these parks.
So that it is abundantly clear I am not singling out the present minister, the previous minister, or any minister for that matter, in respect of this breakdown in communication, let me refer to a report that is commonly called the Crawford report. It was prepared for the department of northern affairs and natural resources respecting certain aspects of these national parks and the townsites therein. It has reference to Banff, Jasper and Waterton Lakes National Parks. It was prepared by Grant Crawford of the Institute of Local Government at Queen's University, Kingston. It was published in 1960. These are some of the statements in the report. At page 9 of the report the following statement is made:
There was a frequently expressed feeling that the inhabitants should have more say in the running of the townsites.
February 10, 1970

This was the feeling expressed in 1959 and 1960, but it certainly has become more common in the last year or two, particularly in the last few months. This report was made under a previous administration. I am not attempting to blame that administration. There has been a breakdown in communications because those of us responsible in Parliament for municipal affairs and local government in these townsites failed to take an adequate interest and failed in our attempt to understand the situation. It is further stated at page 10 of this report:
It is the lack of adequate communication that calls forth such comments as the following: "The immediate problems are first of all autonomy and secondly the relationship of the town to the park superintendent*'; "the local people may believe facilities are desirable but the government will not allow them such things as the drive-in theatre. There should be more local autonomy"; "everything depends on the superintendent. Appeal is only to the minister and you never get answers to letters"-
Again this was in 1959 and 1960. The report goes on to state:
-"in Radium Hot Springs they are rebuilding sewer, water and other works but local people have no say in it and they cannot find out what is happening or even what is proposed"; "no effective means of communication between residents or concessionaires and the parks administration except through the superintendent"; "there was an appeal to the minister from the decisions of the superintendent. What was needed was someone on the spot with power to decide"; "some signs can be approved locally, others must be referred to Ottawa, and a reply may take up to three weeks"; "the machinery is cumbersome and sometimes it takes years to get a decision from Ottawa"; "the superintendent may be very sympathetic but he has not good access to higher authority. The recent visit by the minister and deputy minister was the first in four years. Policy makers have no contact with local problems. They do not spend enough time in the field"; "channels for complaints are inadequate."
This is the situation as described by Professor Crawford in 1959 and 1960. I am sure this situation existed prior to 1957. It is wrong for anyone in this House today to blame this government. Let me reiterate that I am not attempting to blame any government or administration. Those of us who have been in this House have not given enough serious and sincere consideration to the fact that there are people living in Banff and Jasper who are not businessmen. We cannot deal only with land and the question of leases; we must deal with these people as people.
Again, the Crawford report goes on to state at the bottom of page 13:
-if the administration is prepared to go more than half way, the irritation can be greatly reduced.
National Parks Act
It is significant that Professor Crawford indicated it would be necessary for the administration to go more than half way in order that the irritations may be reduced. Unfortunately, in the ten years since the preparation of this report the administration has not seen fit to go anywhere near the halfway position.
I am glad to see that the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) is back in the House. In any event, the result has been a completely deplorable degeneration of communication, trust and goodwill. It is going to take an extreme degree of understanding on our part to resolve this situation so that in years to come we will not have these same problems we have today in relation to national parks before us in this Parliament.
Let me give you an example of this breakdown of goodwill. A few years ago two residents of the parks brought a representative action in the Exchequer Court of Canada seeking a declaration that the perpetual leases they held were in fact intra vires and not ultra vires as the administration had stated.

I am glad the statement of the hon. member is on the record for all the people of Banff and Jasper to see. This is the type of situation which exists. People would believe anything bad of the government. At the same time, the administrators would believe anything bad about the people of Banff and Jasper. They would believe they are all businessmen and gougers. These are not the facts any more than it is a fact that there is any political interference with the Supreme Court of Canada. I mention this because of the breakdown in communication and the complete lack of good will on both sides.
I believe it is time the people of the town-sites got together with the administration to work out a new solution so that the people in the communities would be provided with the same democratic rights enjoyed by others who live outside the area of the national parks. I do not believe such a result will be achieved by this bill unless there are some very significant changes to it. It is my feeling that the townsites of Banff and Jasper should be exempted for the time being from the jurisdiction of the corporation which is to be established. I believe the corporation probably is a very necessary instrument for some of the national parks of Canada. It is probably a very nice instrument for some unpopulated sections of the Banff and Jasper National Parks and for the Waterton National Park. In any event, the head office of such a corporation should be located in Calgary or else-
[Mr. Woolliams.1
where in the province of Alberta where there is the largest volume of problems in relation to national parks. There should be some assurance that persons who are conversant with the business of the national parks would, in fact, be members of the corpora ion.
I believe it would be wrong to apply the operation of this corporation in a blanket fashion to all national parks because this would be a denial of the existence of the communities and people in Banff and Jasper. Banff and Jasper would simply be treated as part of a large body of land. Account would not be taken of the fact that people and communities are in existence there.
I have other reservations about this bill and the powers the corporation would have. Its powers are too wide. The corporation would be in a position to compete with free enterprise in the national parks. Such competition should not be allowed when private enterprise is already in the field. The bill should include guarantees that the corporation would be prevented from coming into competition with private enterprise in this manner. Although there are other changes which I believe must be made, I think most of all there must be a degree of good will on the part of the people in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the people of Banff and Jasper, as well as other communities in the national parks, so that a solution may be found to enable these people to have their own administration completely outside the scope of this bill.
The bill, with the modifications I have mentioned, may be perfectly acceptable to places like Terra Nova National Park, Prince Albert National Park, Wood Buffalo Na ional Park and many others which do not include town-sites and which do not have a permanent population within them; but it is not acceptable to communities such as Banff and Jasper because it denies the existence of people there and will deny to the communities the ordinary relationship enjoyed by people outside the na'ional parks. For this reason, I believe the bill requires extreme modification. I suggest that the parliamentary secretary or the minister should take the time to go to Banff and Jasper in order to discuss this bill thoroughly with the people there before it is passed. In its present form the bill, in my opinion, will not serve the purpose of or be of value to the people of Banff and Jasper.

speechtext:
I would like to make a few comments on Bill C-24. First, I would like to draw to the attention of the House that the Department of

February 10, 1970
Hazardous Products Act National Health and Welfare has done a lot of studies so far as radiation hazards from coloured television sets are concerned. The department has carried on detailed investigations on the problem of radiation from coloured television sets in the past two or three years, and the Minister of National Healh and Welfare (Mr. Munro) has issued public statements from time to lime which gave a clear picture of the investigations as they unfolded. I believe it would be highly appropriate to review this work today before considering in more detail Bill C-24 which we have before us now.
In my opinion, it would be unfortunate if the House were to assume that the appropriate departments were not giving this problem careful attention. The record, as I propose to demonstrate, shows that the Department of Na'ional Health and Welfare, and perhaps other departments as well, have studied this problem closely. This is a highly technical matter in some respects, and in my remarks ihis afternoon I would like to follow through, step by step, the history of this problem as revealed in the public statements made by the ministers of national health and welfare and in rela'ed documents.
We must surely examine these facts very carefully before proceeding to evaluate the merits of the proposal contained in Bill C-24. I say this because the problem of control of radiation from colour television sets, when looked at in depth, is far from being as simple a matter as some members might think on first reading the text of the proposed bill.
The first reference document that I have before me is a news release by the Department of National Health and Welfare dated 10 January 1968, in which the then minister of the department, the hon. Allan J. Mac-Eachen, referred to a study made by the radiation protection division of the department. Apparently, the study he referred to was stimulated by a report emanating from the United States which indicated that certain specific models of colour television receivers had been found to emit excessive amounts of ionizing radiation. The department's study confirmed that these excessive amounts did, in fact, occur in the models mentioned. The problem was limited to large screen models built with a certain chassis, and only those imported from the United States between September 1, 1966 and May 31, 1967 were affected. In these models, high radiation levels were observed adjacent to the shunt-regulator tube, one of the electronic tubes in

the chassis, not the picture tube. The levels were significantly higher than the maximum of 0.5 milliroentgens per hour recommended by the International Commission on Radiological Protection. Incidentally, I should point out that the standard of 0.5 milliroentgens per hour referred to in the statement is apparently the same as the standard suggested in Bill C-24.
In releasing that statement over two years ago, the then minister of national health and welfare emphasized certain significant facts. First of all, the statement makes clear that in carrying out its investigations the department had had the full co-operation of the manufacturer of the faulty television sets. This company was apparently doing everything in its power to track down the particular sets involved and to replace the defective tube with one of a safer design, thus bringing the radiation level within the accepted limit. I note that at the date of the news release, this company had modified, in the manner 1 indicated a moment ago, a total of 3,267 sets. Of all the sets recorded to have come into Canada, only 14 remained uncorrected. There was apparently some difficulty in tracking the last few down, but the report indicated that the department expected that this residual number would be dealt with shortly. Since all this took place over two years ago, I can only assume that this has long since been accomplished.
The second point which was emphasized by the minister of national health and welfare in the same news statement was that his department was checking into the possibility of similar radiation hazards in television sets of other manufacture. Reference was made to correspondence with 14 Canadian manufacturers regarding the nature of the shunt-regulator tube used in their models. At the time of the release, no evidence of any problem similar to the orginal one mentioned a moment ago had been identified, although it is clear in reading the statement that the investigation was continuing.
The general conclusion at this stage of the investigation by the department was that owners of colour television receivers need have little cause for concern about exposure to ionizing radiation. Further, the caution exercised by the television industry in relation to the risks involved seemed to the department to be reasonable and sufficient. There was, however, one note of concern in the statement. While it mentioned that the industry generally was aware of the problem,
February 10, 1970

and most companies were carrying out some form of radiation testing, none appeared to be making detailed tests on shunt-regulator tubes at that time.
The second published statement I have is dated April 10, 1969 and was also a news release from the Department of National Health and Welfare. It quotes the present minister of that department. The minister made the statement in response to inquiries generated by newspaper reports concerning a U.S. survey which had been taken in New York state. This survey had indicated that potentially dangerous radiation had been emitted above the recommended level of 0.5 milliroentgens per hour.
Apparently this report came as a surprise to the department. The minister said that since 1967, when the incident to which I referred a moment ago occurred, the radiation protection division of the department had been checking radiation levels of new model television receivers as these new models were introduced. They had checked 61 different models of 17 different companies. The tests had ensured that the sets, as marketed, did not emit radiation in excess of the standard level. As I understand it, only one set of each model was actually tested, the purpose of the test being to assure that the design of the set and its components was such as to eliminate the radiation emission. It was assumed that all sets of this model would behave the same in this respect.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
The statement I am still referring to, the news release of April 10, 1969, then goes on to hint at a possible explanation for the high radiation levels found in the U.S. survey report. It noted that it had been found that sometimes sets which had been modified, subsequent to sale to the customer, could be potentially dangerous. This was because modifications involving an increase in the voltage applied to certain components could give rise to an increased level of radiation. The department recommended that such increases in the high-voltage settings should not be made, and although it believed that the associated radiation fields would be hazardous only over long periods of exposure, it stated that it was extending its testing program to ensure that, while in the past the department had been concerned with the safety of sets going on to the market, it now realized that servicing modifications or repairs might be made to the sets after purchase, and that the effect of these operations had to be investigated.
Hazardous Products Act
Now, Mr. Speaker, at the end of this news release is a statement of particular significance in relation to the bill which is before us at the present time, and with your permission I will quote two or three sentences:
It is recognized that there is an increasing use of products capable of emitting potentially hazardous radiation. These include, besides t.v. sets. X-ray equipment, microwave generators and lasers. The minister added that his department is therefore seeking suitable regulatory powers to establish minimum safety standards for such equipment sold in Canada.
I believe that the sequel to that stated intention is the Radiation Emitting Devices Bill which has recently received second reading in the Senate. It would appear that, even at that time, the department was prudently preparing to establish safety regulations for colour t.v. sets if it should become necessary-although at that stage of the investigation, at any rate, there was no clear indication that they would be necessary.
Two weeks later, on April 24, 1969, the Minister of National Health and Welfare announced plans for a national sampling survey of colour t.v. sets in people's homes. This announcement also was in the form of a news release. The minister referred again to reports from the United States which indicated that some sets in use in people's homes emitted above the standard level. Set owners in Canada were invited to participate in a survey to be carried out by the Radiation Protection Division of the department. They would be supplied with a radiographic film pack which they were to attach to the outside of their sets and return it to the division after 20 hours of viewing time. The survey would be conducted according to a statistical pattern to provide sampling of a wide range of makes and models. The survey would be carried out by mail-the necessary material and instructions to do the test exposure would be sent to the participant.
This survey was in fact carried out. I understand that over 2,000 citizens wrote to the department and offered to participate in the survey. Of these, 400 were chosen by the department to carry out the radiation testing. On August 6, 1969, the minister released a report on the results of the tests on the 400 sets. The results are given in the form of a table appended to the news release. The 400 sets were analysed in four categories, with about 100 sets in each category. The categories related to the year in which the set was purchased, 1969, 1968, 1967, and 1966 or earlier. About 20 per cent of sets purchased in

February 10, 1970
Hazardous Products Act
1966	or earlier emitted radiation which, in some degree, exceeded the standard of 0.5 milliroentgen per hour recommended by the International Commission on Radiological Protection. The proportion fell to 14 per cent in
1967	models, 8 per cent in 1968 and 4 per cent in 1969. In most of the cases where emission was above the standard, it was only slightly above the accepted standard. Examination of the table of results does reveal, however, that at least three of the 400 sets emitted at rates of more than ten times the standard.
In presenting these results, the minister emphasized that the study had been of an exploratory nature only and that these results had not been followed up in detail. The department was not able to state whether or not the higher levels occurred only in certain specific models. It could not say whether the excessive emissions were due to occasional failures in quality control during manufacture, to regional variations in line voltage, to alterations made by repairmen or to a combination of such factors.
In discussing the results, the report stated that the health hazard, even where radiation emission was above the standard, was considered by the department to be exceedingly small. The standard carried such a high safety margin that, unless it were exceeded by a substantial amount, any health risk would be quite insignificant. It pointed out that the radiation emission was observed only at the point of closest approach to the electronic tubes, at the side, back or bottom of the set, not in the normal viewing position. Thus, the exposure of the viewer could be considered negligible if a normal viewing distance, preferably four feet or more, were maintained. The report then goes on to give a warning that prolonged proximity to the side or back of a set should be avoided as much as possible.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I have before me a news release of the Department of National Health and Welfare dated September 4, 1969, and titled "Safety Rules for Colour TV Users." In this statement the minister gave further information relating to the studies made by his department on colour T.V. hazards. He referred to the survey that had been carried out and noted that about 10 per cent of the sets tested had been found to emit radiation somewhat in excess of the accepted manufacturing standard. Examples of such sets had been found among all popular makes, the largest number being among the models purchased before 1967. The causes
[Mr. Haidasz.l
were complex and attributed partly to component design and partly to servicing.
The minister repeated that, in the opinion of his department, these radiation-emitting sets were not a significant health hazard if given the usual degree of respect accorded many other household appliances. The radiation was observed only at the back, bottom or sides of the sets, not in the normal viewing position and this, coupled with the very large safety margin inherent in the accepted standard, made the health hazard extremely small.
e (5:20 p.m.)
The news release then proceeded to give simple rules which would ensure safety even in cases where radiation emission was somewhat in excess of the accepted manufacturing standard. One of these rules is to consult your authorized repairman rather than attempting to do your own servicing. Another is to ask the repairman, on his next servicing call, to check the voltage regulating circuits and radiation shielding as specified by the manufacturer. Another rule is to cultivate good viewing habits-to not regularly sit closer than four feet from the set or to allow children to he with legs extended beneath the set while viewing. And lastly, to place all colour television sets against a wall and not to locate chairs immediately adjacent to the side or back.
