Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak very briefly on this proposed measure, Bill C-24. I should like to see it passed by the House and referred to the Standing Committee. I take this position because I am one of a number of members interested in possible colour television fires, and the number of fatalities arising from them. I first became interested in 1968 after reading statistics concerning explosions in colour Television sets in the United States. I took it upon myself to raise the matter in questions in the House, and in correspondence wiih the Department of National Health and Welfare, asking that a check be made into the situation. I also corresponded with people whom I considered to be very knowledgeable on the subject. Some months ago, the Department of National Health and Welfare decided to take a second look at the relationship between coloured television sets and fires, and fatalities caused by such fires.
While my interest in the subject is a little different from that of the mover of the bill, I think there is a common denominator. Here, we are dealing with colour television operation, fires and other hazards that may result from same, which is a new and unsolved problem. While the department is taking a second look at the fires caused by the small percentage of sets involved, I think the endor-sation of Bill C-24 and its reference to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs would be a practical and complementary step to take.
Without further discussion on my part, Mr. Speaker, I hope the House will see fit to refer this bill to the committee.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have an opportunity to speak to this bill which relates to a matter of considerable importance and one which has been of increasing concern to the general public. It has also occupied the attention of television manufacturers and the various health authorities over a considerable period of time. The fact that I have one of the large national and international manufacturers in my riding explains my particular interest.
Hazardous Products Act
Any matter which affects or could potentially affect the health of Canadian citizens is certainly worthy of discussion in this chamber. I should like to congratulate the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) for introducing this bill.
You could do a lot better by letting it go to the committee.

We have heard from the parliamentary secretary who has indicated the acaon taken by the Department of National Health and Welfare in the investigation of possible hazards from colour television sets. Perhaps I could go a little further into the question and try to evaluate the situation in the light of the information we have, and to relate it to the proposal put forward in the bill we are considering. To do this in a systematic way, I will address myself to three basic questions that come to mind and which must be answered before we can assess the merits of the bill.
The first and most fundamental question is: Is it true that colour television sets present a health hazard? The second question is: If so, what is the real nature of the hazard? And finally: If there is a health hazard, is the procedure suggested in the bill the most appropriate way of controlling the problem? I will deal with each of these matters separately, in turn.
Now, with respect to the first question, Mr. Speaker, are colour television sets dangerous? Everyone will be aware that there have been from time to time some very frightening accounts in the public press and in the news media. In some cases there may have been an element of deliberate sensationalism involved in these accounts, but in the main they were clearly attempts by responsible members of the news media to give a simplified account of what is, in fact, a highly technical problem-namely, the effects produced by radiation on the human body. The emphasis in these accounts was on the possibility of an increase in the incidence of leukemia and cancer and an increase in the number of births of deformed children. These are, of course, the known effects of excessive exposure to x-rays. I am sure that it was with these dire effects in mind that the bill we have before us was introduced by the hon member for St. John's East.
There is no doubt that stories such as these have aroused a large measure of concern among all sectors of the public. That is why, Mr. Speaker, I was interested in reading in a popular publication the TV Guide, issue of

February 10, 1970
Hazardous Products Act 13-19 December, 1969, a feature article which purports to reveal "the facts behind the frightening headlines". Many members of this House may have read this article also. My copy came from the cash counter of a local supermarket and, being on display there, the publication undoubtedly has wide circulation. The article tries, in a sense, to debunk the idea that colour television is dangerous. The author, Mr. David Lachenbruch, has quoted statements made by many reputable scientists and public health officials in the United States. He has marshalled these statements in such a way as to support the proposition that there is almost no risk whatsoever.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
For example, Mr. Speaker, the article reports that Dr. Lauriston-Taylor, president of the National Commission on Radiological Protection-that is the United States national commission-told a congressional committee that exposure as much as two million times the half-milliroentgen standard for television sets would not even produce skin irritation if applied to a small area of the body, and that in 30 years there had not been a single case of identifiable injury to an individual by low-level x-rays of the kind emitted by defective television sets.
It also reported that Professor Hanson Blatz, the radiation control director for New York city, told a congressman that viewing a set which radiated 24 times as much as the interna, ional standard for five hours a day at 22 feet from the screen would expose the viewer to no more radiation than a resident of Denver normally gets with no television viewing at all. He concludes that the probability of detectable medical effects from x-rays emitted by faulty colour receivers is vanishingly small.
The article goes on to quote Dr. Victor P. Bond, associate director of Brookhaven National Laboratory, to the effect that even if the standard were exceeded 10 to 20 times, the doses and dose ra'es would still be very low, and that no medical effects have ever been demonstrated at such levels. It also refers to statements made by the greater New York chapter of the Health Physics Society. This society is said to have regarded the half-milliroentgen limit as having no relationship to the probability of injury to individuals; that there is no evidence to suggest that injury to individuals is likely even for chronic exposure at many times this intensity.
There are other categorical statements in the article, Mr. Speaker, that are not attribut-

ed to any named source. For example, there is the statement that a set emitting the maximum amount of radiation, that is, the half-milliroentgen or half-millirem limit, would expose the viewer to less than 5 per cent of the average amount of normal background radiation; and in a similar context, the statement that most luminous dial watches give off twice as much radiation as does a television set emitting at the maximum limit recommended by the National Commission on Radiological Protection.
These opinions, taken together, would seem to indicate that there is really no problem at all to be concerned with. I do not wish to suggest that the article gives a completely one-sided view of the question, but that is certainly the main theme that emerges. In fact, in summing up the discussion the author quotes the opinion of John C. Villforth, director of the Bureau of Radiological Health, Department of Health, Education and Welfare in the United States. His position on the subject was apparently given at an annual meeting of the American Public Health Association and would seem to be quite categorical. The quoted remark is: "There is no danger in colour T.V. I am confident. If you are at all apprehensive, seek the advice of your serviceman."
On the surface, this would appear to completely dispose of the concern that has been expressed elsewhere and which has led to the introduction of the bill we are considering. However, let us now compare this conclusion with the statements made by the Department of National Health and Welfare which were referred to earlier in this debate. The position of the department, as expressed by the minister in a news release, is that the health hazard of colour television sets is extremely small and that it can be considered negligible if viewing is conducted in normal viewing position. So far so good. However, the news release goes on to modify this assurance by adding that it is undesirable to remain in prolonged close proximity to the side or back of a set while it is operating. This then is where the real concern lies.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if we were to go back to Mr. Lachenbruch's article in the TV Guide, and examine the statements somewhat more critically, we would find that there is really no discrepancy between the opinions of the eminent United States authorities it quotes and those of the Department of National Health and Welfare. It will be clear on careful reading of the statements of the United
February 10, 1970

States authorities that they were referring to normal viewing conditions, a few feet in front of the set. Our Department of National Health and Welfare says that if such distances are maintained, the risk to health is extremely small, even if the set emits at a rate somewhat in excess of the standard. So there is agreement on this point.
However, our health department goes on to warn that prolonged proximity to the back or sides of a set is undesirable in view of the fact that emission rates in excess of the standard do occur for various reasons. This is likewise the opinion of some U.S. experts quoted in the article to which I referred. For example, Dr. Karl Z. Morgan, director of the Health Physics Division of the Oak Ridge National Laboratory is reported to endorse the watch-at-a-distanee advice, noting particularly that "many children lie on the floor with their feet immediately under the colour television sets and with their faces almost glued to the screen for many hours of viewing". Furthermore, the U.S. Surgeon General has issued viewing rules for colour set owners that are essentially identical to the rules given by our Department of National Health and Welfare in one of its news releases, and these rules emphasize the desirability of maintaining a reasonable distance in front of the set when it is operating.
There is another point in the reassuring statements quoted by Mr. Lachenbruch that needs comment. Much is made of the fact that no identifiable injury has ever been reported and that no medical effects have been demonstrated. I am informed that these statements are literally true, but that the key words are "identifiable" and "demonstrated". Our Department of National Health and Welfare has repeatedly said that radiation effects are of a statistical nature, so that it is enormously difficult or impossible to demonstrate a direct connection between low-level radiation exposures and the occurrence of disease in a particular individual, even though connection has been demonstrated, somewhat indirectly if you like, and in two other ways: by research on animals, by extrapolation of the effects observed in human populations at high levels of exposure.
I think it is clear from what I have been saying, Mr. Speaker, that the hazard, although small, cannot be completely discounted. However, it is equally clear that the hazard exists only if there is prolonged proximity to the side or back of the set, not if it is simply viewed in the normal viewing position. One could argue that there is, thus, no 21701-8J
Hazardous Products Act hazard if the set is used in the manner intended, or reasonably anticipated, by the manufacturer; and one could well ask whether such a hazard should be subject to control by the government. Mr. Speaker, many things in the home are dangerous if not used with a certain degree of respect. A carving knife is a dangerous instrument, and there is some risk associated with almost all electrical appliances.
However, I think there is a distinct difference in the case we are considering. I will give two reasons for this: first, the fact that the hazard is from radiation makes it especially insidious. Radiation cannot be detected by any human sense and this is the reason we find it so frightening. It can be detected only by an expert armed with proper equipment. The second point I would call attention to is that television is becoming a focal point of family life. We and our children live in intimate association with our television sets for many hours each day. Therefore, even if the risk is exceedingly small, we must be sure that it has been reduced to the very lowest level that is technically feasible.
In fact, we may say that a television set that emits radiation is contributing to pollution of the environment-the home environment. Mr. Lachenbruch, in the article I referred to earlier, makes this point. He says that environmental scientists feel that nonuseful radiation should be blocked and not permitted to add to the background level. We know that already there exists a substantial radiation background from such things as radioactive fall-out, cosmic rays, luminous dials, etc. Environmental scientists want to hold this background radiation to a minimum because of its collective potential to civilization as a whole.
e (5:40 p.m.)
In this connection, Mr. Speaker, I am reminded that it is the environmental scientists in the Department of National Health and Welfare who have had most to do with the studies mentioned earlier in this debate. There is an environmental health directorate in the department which deals with pollution of various kinds, including radiation pollution. Like scientists all over the world, they are concerned with increases in the radiation background, especially that produced by the increased use of technical devices in our modern technological society. People in this modern day absorb considerably more radiation from various sources than did their

February 10, 1970
Hazardous Products Act forefathers. This is a worrisome development. Each new technological advance, if it involves a radiation device, contributes to the increase in the radiation pollution of the environment. Inevitably, this will lead at some point to the necessity for governmental regulation and control.
It is on these very general grounds that I could perhaps support the idea of control regulations for colour television sets, if necessary and feasible. This leads me to the final question of the three that I asked at the beginning. If we grant that some form of government regulation is necessary, is the present bill the most appropriate way of dealing with the problem? Let us look at this carefully.
What is proposed in the bill is an amendment to the Hazardous Products Act which would prevent the sale of television sets which emit radiation above the standard. A regulation of this kind may be effective in achieving the desired objective, or it may not. It would seem, according to the Lachenbruch article and the health department's news release, that most of the sets found to emit over the standard did so as a result of changes introduced during servicing operations. In both the United States and Canada sample, sets tested before sale checked out all right. It was only in sets examined after a period of use, when they had presumably received servicing to replace worn-out tubes, that excessive emission was noted.
It is true there were new sets which emitted over the standard back in 1967, but this was due to defective tubes in certain models. Since then the manufacturers have made many improvements and are checking their products more closely. The result is that there is now no indication whatsoever that any of the new sets placed on the market emit over the standard. This is not to say they will not do so later if they are improperly serviced, but my point is that the proposal in the bill would not prevent that kind of mishap in any even.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, according to Mr. Lachenbruch's article, manufacturers are making even further improvements which are designed to make servicing foolproof during the entire life of a set. They are doing this by introducing fail-safe electronic systems which are being gradually phased into production. Many manufacturers are doing away with the tubes which can cause radiation, replacing them with new types of solid-state components which cannot radiate. Others have

improved shielding around critical circuits. Even the glass in picture tubes is being reformulated to provide greater resistance to x-rays. The question arises as to whether it is desirable to introduce government regulation while such developments are in progress.
If the proposed regulation were made, how would it be enforced? New designs appear to check out all right on randomly-selected samples. The difficulty lies in the possibility of failure in quality control which would result in some sets going onto the market with emission rates higher than the general rim. It is not clear how the proposed regulation would prevent this kind of mishap or even bring it to light. Much would depend on the way the regulation was implemented. Then again, the technical specifications which would constitute the standard need consideration. I understand that in the United States, where similar regulatory action has been proposed, the proposed regulation is lengthy, complicated and highly technical.
I think the whole question needs a close examination by technical experts. A regulation that is not technically sound and based on the latest knowledge of the situation might do more harm than good and would perhaps lead to unproductive effort on the part of both the manufacturers and the regulatory authorities while doing no service to the public. As I understand it, the Department of National Health and Welfare is in close contact with the problem in all its technical aspects and has been so from the beginning. The minister can be expected to take whatever action is most advisable in full knowledge of all the circumstances.
Mr. Speaker, I, too, would like to congratulate the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath-
I am touched, Mr. Speaker; deeply moved.
-for introducing a subject which is very appropriate for discussion in this House, especially during this hour. One of the purposes of private members' hour-
-is certainly not to pass legislation!

-is to call the attention of the public to matters which in the opinion of hon. members are worthy of public debate and should be considered as a possible basis for legislative action. The hon. member has
February 10, 1970

called attention to the hazards presented by colour television sets. I understand a bill has been introduced in the other place, Bill S-14, which is broader in scope and which would probably include the question under discussion. I regret that the mover of this motion did not take the opportunity to tell us more about the reasons which impelled him to put this measure before us.
As I say, we have an opportunity in the Parliament of Canada, particularly at this hour, to call for public debate. Public debate is the basis for the formation of public opinion, the basis upon which measures might ultimately become the policy of the government. In debates such as these, ideas are put forward and tested, and the logic which hon. members contribute in the course of their deliberations is put to rigorous examination.
1 listened with great interest to the hon. member for Surrey (Mr. Mather), the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) and the hon. member for Kitchener (Mr. Hymmen). The hon. member for Surrey, like the hon. member who moved this motion, intervened only briefly in the debate. It is clear that this is a matter which calls for careful consideration. There have been reports in the press of potential radiation hazards, as well as of a potential fire hazard, as the hon. member for Surrey pointed out. The hon. member for Kitchener made some useful comments, calling attention to the fact that investigation into this problem did not simply mean an examination of the technical features of radiation; it is broader than that.
Colour television has come to be an essential part of Canadian family life in large areas of this country. My family acquired a colour television set last year and I was astonished at the nature of the response of members of the family to it. As Professor Scanlon of Carleton University stated, colour television leaves a different impression qualitatively. Family reaction to advertising, for example, is significantly different in a sociological sense; the impression left on young minds is deeper and more lasting. We cannot ignore the fact that we are dealing with something which is very much entrenched our way of living.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
As the hon. member for Kitchener stated, it is doubtful whether the correct way of dealing with this difficulty is to pay attention simply to the standard of the product as it leaves the factory. Effective supervision would seem
Hazardous Products Act to call not only for technical supervision of manufacturing operations but for inspection on delivery, installation and the work of service and repair, as well as periodic testing to make sure there is no deterioration of components likely to result in hazard while in use. Not least, there is need for a program of public education to train viewers in good television habits. The set should probably be placed against the wall. There should be a minimum distance between viewer and set. As has been pointed out, children are sometimes accustomed to lying around with their feet underneath the set in an area where, if there is a radiation hazard, the hazard would be at its maximum. Careful viewing habifs, careful servicing habits and a major public education program: these are the measures that have to be considered in addition merely to limiting, as proposed by the hon. member.
I am confident that we have not heard the end of this kind of proposal, which is a very serious one indeed and well worthy of debate. I am confident, too, that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) is as acutely aware of the problem as any member of this House. I have before me a series of press releases dealing with colour television, the latest in December of last year. They relate to reports on the hazards of colour television sets and to investigations that have been conducted, as described by the hon. member for Parkdale, with the co-operation of some 400 families, who assisted in making a survey of viewing habits and the performance of television sets in a number of Canadian homes.
It is clear that there has been a marked improvement in the quality of sets that are now being produced by the manufacturers. Year by year the number of defective sets in the sense of those that emit radiation has been reduced. It is quite clear that there is a substantial measure of voluntary compliance by the industry, as the hon. member for Kitchener pointed out. Much still remains to be done.
Again I wish to commend the hon. member for introducing this measure. I hope that when the matter comes before the House again he will give us the benefit, in a more extended way, of his views as well as a recital of the events that motivated him to bring the measure before the House.

I plead for flexibility in our parks system. It is rather awkward to even suggest this, but I plead for a measure of autonomy for the permanent residents of our parks. I plead, also, for the preservation of a large part of our nation for the use of our citizens. It may be that we are rapidly reaching the point of no return in this regard. Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this bill I would suggest that the principle enshrined in it makes it a very bad and undesirable piece of legislation. I believe the principle should be established that the minister and his department should be directly responsible to the public whom they serve.
This bill is simply a device to enable the government to avoid answering for its actions. It is a buffer between the real park proprietors and those members of the public affected by the policies they lay down. The new Crown corporation will not be a free agent; it will be a creature of the cabinet. Yet the minister concerned will always be able to wiggle out of answering legitimate questions in the House by claiming he cannot interfere in the affairs of an autonomous agency established by Parliament. It will be yet another page in the frustrating story so well illustrated by the CBC, the National Film Board and the like.
The question of national parks in Canada is preponderantly one of concern to the people of western Canada because that is where all the park land to speak of is situated. As recently as two years ago, 86 per cent of all national parkland was in the west. Yet the control of that land lies in central Canada. Policy is established here in Ottawa and administered by officials, many of whom know a national park only as an area on the map. This is a flagrant example of absentee landlordism at its worst. It is comparable to what happened in Eire in the last century.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
The federal government controls this land entirely, yet it does not want the bother of looking after maintenance and collecting rents. The government has done what the worst absentee landlords have always done throughout history-named an agent to do the dirty work and stand as a buffer between its comfortable existence and the irate tenants.
I have a letter from a resident of Lake Louise who charges that the director of parks has spent only a few days in the west, but he will have considerable say in the affairs of people who are directly dependent upon the good operation of the park areas for their living. This letter was sent by Mr. Jack McDowall of Lake Louise to the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale).
With more than three-quarters of the national parkland in the west, and the dictatorial control of its destiny held firmly in Ottawa, is it any wonder that westerners are sceptical of the treatment they and their parkland will receive? Is it any wonder, Mr. Speaker, that westerners are more and more coming to doubt the benefits to them and to their area of staying in a constitutional set-up where they are repeatedly ignored and their rights and interests continually slighted in deference to the interests of central and eastern Canada? This sort of legislation is just another open invitation to secession, another example of prejudice and discrimination.
The evils of this type of remote control are not too hard to find. Such administrative methods are bound to lead to mistakes and to inappropriate action. Areas have been mishandled and are still being mishandled due to this cumbersome and distant system of control. One good example is in my own province of Manitoba. Riding Mountain National Park should not be maintained in its present role of wilderness reserve. Instead,

February 10, 1970

new areas to the north, and away from the march of development, should be taken for this purpose.
Riding Mountain National Park was made over to the federal authority in the late 1920s at a time when no one had a very clear idea of what a national park should be. Now most Canadian provinces have clear-cut parkland policies, sound programs of development and maintenance and a good understanding of the recreational needs of their populations. They have tremendous know-how and experience. I believe Riding Mountain National Park could well be turned back to the province of Manitoba and a fresh area taken up for wilderness preservation.
This park is situated slap in the middle of a well-built and developed area and astride an important provincial road link. It is 70 miles deep and 30 miles wide. This huge area inhibits development of a tremendous area of central Manitoba and makes the social and business life of the region unnecessarily difficult because of the wide detours that its wilderness state makes necessary. Highway No. 10 runs through the middle, but the park part of the road is in such poor shape that travellers are forced to skirt the park and make wide detours. If this were a provincial park it could accommodate recreational facilities, reasonably good roads and appropriate commercial enterprises. Now it is a dead area in the centre of a developed region of great potential.
The present national parks policy is not suited to Riding Mountain Park as it is situated. The area is not a mountain at all but is really an escarpment, a plateau that should form a natural part of the agricultural community surrounding it. From the days of the fur traders the park has been traversed by people, but now people are prevented from going back and forth easily through the park. The problem posed by this park is only one of the many faced by westerners who must look to a distant and disinterested administration in Ottawa for answers. The Crown corporation that this bill seeks to set up will simply add another layer to the protection afforded the government by the rigid and dictatorial bureaucracy that we have had so far.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I think the present parks policy of wilderness, so far as it concerns the Riding Mountain National Park, is very ill-suited to that area. Not all parks can be treated the same if we are to have any reasonable development of our parks at the
National Parks Act
national level. For these reasons I disagree entirely with the principle of this bill.

Mr. Speaker, earlier today we heard an important announcement by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to the effect that the government was proposing to set up an information bureau that would be known as Information Canada. According to the Prime Minister's statement, one of the purposes of Information Canada is to hear the views of the people of Canada and their reaction to public policy.
The other afternoon when this bill was brought before the House, the members of the opposition took a firm stand, to the point of moving the adjournment of the debate because of the absence of the minister from the House. The Prime Minister was careful to point out that the new information bureau the government is proposing would serve the purpose not only of distributing information to the people of Canada and hearing their views, but of listening to the views of hon. members of this House, the elected representatives of the people.
It is quite obvious that the minister, who is conspicuous by his absence tonight, is not going to pay the slightest heed to anything that is said in this chamber. By the same token, it seems obvious that the statement of the Prime Minister this afternoon about Information Canada is so much hypocrisy, because it is fundamental to the democratic process and to the parliamentary process that a minister's first responsibility is to listen to the tenor, the tone and the content of debate in this House and that government decisions be influenced accordingly. There is not much we can do about it now, I suppose. It will be taken care of by the electorate of Canada in due course. However, I think it is the duty of members who will take part in this debate to protest as strongly as they can this ministerial arrogance, which I submit is tantamount to the old adage, "Don't confuse me with the facts: my mind is already made up."

He will not accept the basic principle of democracy, namely, the right of self-determination. The same situation prevails with respect to Eskimos in northern Quebec who have let it be known that they are being denied their traditional rights and protection of the department and are forced to cross to the Northwest Territories, particularly to Cape Dorset.
The minister is in difficulty over the question of sovereignty in northern Canada, and with respect to greater autonomy in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories because he will not listen to the vox populi and to the people who are most concerned with policy matters in his department.
This evening I want to deal with one or two matters that have been raised already in the course of the debate which were deliberate attempts to distort the record with respect to the past policy on national parks. This process of distortion was begun by the minister

when he tabled a letter a few weeks ago in the House which he claimed indicated that the arrogant, autocratic and bureaucratic policy set down in the bill that is now before the House-and which is represented by the attitude of the minister-was begun at the time I had responsibility for the administration of the parks of Canada. This problem affects particularly the national parks of western Canada and is further discrimination on the part of the government against a region of Canada which is already in a very serious state of alienation because of the arbitrary action of the present Liberal administration. One of the reasons for this feeling of alienation and isolation is that the government refuses to listen to the responsible representations of the people who live in the western provinces. Whenever the responsible voice of the westerner is heard with regard to the national parks, the minister and other spokesmen for the goverment immediately apply the red herring tactic by suggesting that it is only the avaricious, commercial interests who wish to preserve the traditional rights of the western national parks.
Let me point out, so there will be no mistake in this matter, that western Canada has the real need for the preservation, conservation and wise management of our natural resources has been recognized. There are no national parks in the province of Quebec. There are only minor national parks in the province of Ontario. Why? Because those provinces are not willing to make available the land that would be required for national parks purposes. There has been a tentative suggestion that the government of Quebec would make land available in the Gaspe, but on the basis of special privileges such as a 99-year lease rather than surrendering it to the Federal Crown in perpetuity.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
Let there be no mistake about this matter. Western Canada is accused of being avaricious and predatory with respect to its natural resources. I would give the lie to that statement by indicating that it is only in western Canada that huge areas of land have been made available in the interests of the preservation of these resources for the present and future generations of Canadians, as the National Parks Act specifies.
There are also parks in the maritime provinces, but there is no leasehold problem there.

In the early days when parks were first established in the west, population was comparatively small but distances were great. Town-sites were already established, particularly in Banff and Jasper, which made it necessary for the government, in coming to terms with the provincial authorities on the development of national parks, to provide for leaseholds in perpetuity.
I want to deal with the question of perpetual leaseholds because it is the essence of the complaint that has been bothering the residents, particularly of the mountain parks, during the past few years. speechtext:
So much for Information Canada. God help the people of Canada with this sort of nonsense going on amongst their elected representatives.
Mr. Speaker, there is certainly need for the implementation of a comprehensive plan for our national parks which meets the problems well known by everyone concerned with these matters; that is, the increase in leisure time, population explosion, mobility created by roads and cars, and the impact of tourism.
In 1963 the former administration announced a policy which was designed to adapt the parks to the changing circumstances and needs of the people. At the same time it was necessary to operate on the basis of the proposals that came out of the Resources for Tomorrow Conference, that is, wise management and multiple use. Essential to the plan was the setting up within the department of a planning division which, as I have already intimated, was to review development in each of the western parks-this is essen ially a western problem-and to come up with a master plan that would see the adequate development of the parks to the end of the century.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Basic to the plan was a zoning policy which would consist of three zones. The townsite or service centre would deal with the problems of Banff and Jasper, permanent townsites, and also with some of the other western parts where there are substantial service centres that operate during the summer months. There would be a buffer zone which would provide camping facilities for the people who wished to get into the recreative environment of the national parks. Finally, there would be a wilderness zone which would remain in a completely undeveloped, wilderness state. This would ensure the preservation of these
National Parks Act
unique land areas, flora and fauna, for all future generations.
A vital part of the plan was that it would be in touch with regional needs because Canada is a big country with different regional requirements. There is provision for the decentralization of administration. An office was established in Calgary for the purpose of coming to a closer realization of the particular needs of the western national parks. So that there might be autonomy in the town-sites, town managers were appointed in order to relieve the superintendents of the park areas from the responsibility of administering the problems of the townsites.
There were also plans afoot for new national parks, because the number of national parks, in the face of the growing demand, must be doubled immediately if we are to meet the needs of our people for recreational facilities. Terra Nova, Newfoundland, and a new national park in Nova Scotia were established. Negotiations were under way for parks in the Northwest Territories, Yukon, and for the preservation of that unique land in southwestern Saskatchewan, the cypress hills prairie lands, the home of the prairie dog, as extolled in the old song, where the deer and the antelope play.
There has been no real progress along these lines in the last seven years except for repeated announcement that new national parks will be developed. A federal-provincial parks conference was established so there would be continuous communication between the federal and provincial authorities. It is primarily a provincial problem, involving alienation of provincial land. The provinces of On' ario and Quebec are reluctant to permit the alienation of their land to the Crown. Little wonder, for we have a minister who refuses to accept his responsibility for listening to the advice and helpful information that hon. members concerned with these problems can offer.
More important still, again arising out of the Resources for Tomorrow Conference of 1961, a private group was established concerned with our national and provincial parks. We now have a Provincial and Federal Parks Association which has been making an excellent contribution to the on-going discussion concerning the preservation of our park resources.
To indicate that there was some public approval of the plan, an editorial in the Albertan of January 25, 1963, following the announcement of the program that I have

February 10. 1970
National Parks Act
outlined briefly tonight was headed, "Bravo, Mr. Dinsdale!". The editorial wholly endorsed the plan which was laid down at that time. There was a similar editorial in the Calgary Herald. Both these editorials arose from the fact that the announcement was made in the province of Alberta which perhaps has the largest land area devoted to national parks.
The situation has deteriorated sadly since that time. The government has arbitrarily cancelled perpetual leases. A parliamentary committee went to the mountain parks three or four years ago and for three days listened to the voice of the people there. I thought they made a convincing case, but the government decided otherwise and came up with this leasehold Crown corporation as a solution to a problem that was becoming embarrassing to the government. Incidentally, this is not a new act. It was first proposed in 1967, as I recall, before the last election. Because it was politically embarrassing, the government decided not to proceed with it. I am aware of the voice of the people of the Rocky Mountain constituency which is opposed to what the government is now suggesting. Surely, the voice of the people of Canada should take priority over the task forces, the commissions, royal commissions, Information Canada and all the other administrative bodies which have no authority or responsibility to the people of Canada. Surely, the voice of the people is much more important than these faceless bodies.

Because of the arbitrary administrative decree which removed a fundamental right of the people of the parks which had been granted by the Crown, the people took the matter to the Exchequer Court. The Exchequer Court upheld the rights of the people. Now the minister, great democrat that he is, has taken this question to the Supreme Court of Canada to try to have the opinion reversed. The latest controversy revolves around the exhorbitant increase in leasehold rentals to which I have already made reference. My friend the parliamentary secretary disputes the figures. Unfortunately, I do not have time to go into a detailed analysis; but as was pointed out in the letter which I read, the residents of the park are quite happy with the provincial assessment rates as the basis. They are the ones affected by the exhorbitant figures to which I have already referred.
The protests of the people of the national parks is a western protest. Surely, the government is not so insensitive to the problem of national unity in this country that it refuses to regard this as a special regional problem in the west. An article in the January 16, 1970, edition of the Calgary Herald is headed, "Chretien tells Banff 'Like it or Leave'." There is real, responsible democracy for you!
My time is rapidly coming to an end. I want to indicate that there is a need for change and reform with respect to the administration of the western national parks. I think the other provinces should come into the national parks system. We need a rapid increase in the number of national parks available. We need recreational parks. There was a program all set to roll which would have provided financial assistance to the provinces to expand their recreational parks network.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
In addition, in the light of the unhappy experience in our western national parks, we need to reinforce the zoning principles laid down in 1963 so that there could be a special category of parks which might well be called national wilderness parks. The zoning principle was designed to prevent any further deterioration of the wilderness in the western parks. Westerners, above all others, realize the importance of preserving this aspect of our national resources. The boundaries of wilderness parks and the zoning in national parks have to be established by legislation because, obviously, the government cannot be
February 10, 1970

trusted to adhere to policies which it has itself enunciated in the past.
The townsites require special administration, which again ought to be dealt with by special legislation. Banff and Jasper were towns before they were included in national parks. Surely, it is the essence of bureaucracy gone mad to try to ignore the fact that Canadians live within the national parks in townsites, on a permanent basis. They, too, are entitled to the same rights as all Canadians. They are not avaricious. They are not seeking personal aggrandizement. Indeed, they are in the forefront of those who insist that the national parks be preserved and developed in accordance with the highest possible standards.
In addition to the zoning, which has been accepted by the residents in the national parks, I think we should become seriously concerned about the establishment of national seashore sanctuaries. This demand is given even greater urgency by what is happening off the coast of Nova Scotia today. We should also be preserving the primitive wilderness along the course of some of our great national rivers. These are the things we should be concerned about, instead of becoming bureaucratically involved in further removing the fundamental rights of Canadians who live in the national parks of Canada, people who have developed those parks and made a unique contribution to the quality of Canadian life everywhere in so doing. Some of them have made this their life's work. Now, because of this arbitrary legislation, they are likely to see it swept away, not even by elected parliamentary representatives but by faceless figures operating under the protection of a Crown corporation.
I know this attempt to get a response from the government is like shouting into the wind, because when it comes to western members the government has demonstrated time and time again that it has not the slightest intention of listening to the elected representatives of the people. I plead with the government, in the interest of peace, order and good government in this country, to listen. It is not good enough for the minister responsible for developing this important aspect of public policy to absent himself from the House because he does not want to listen to the elected representatives.
I began by pointing out that Information Canada amounts to so much nonsense and possesses all the ominous overtones of an effort by a government arrogant long before

its time to develop a propaganda machine which will confuse the issue to such an extent that the people will scarcely know what their rights and privileges are.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be short. Many people in my constituency are concerned about the form of the developments taking place in our national parks, particularly in the national park at Waskesiu in Prince Albert National Park. They are concerned, as I suppose all Canadians are, about overcrowding, the influx of cars and the increased use of facilities that is going to be the fate of our national parks, particularly the one that we have in northern Saskatchewan.
Changes are already under way. The park has been developed over the years and the people there lived in very modest residences such as shacks, summer cottages, and so on. Recent policy seeks to change this situation. The change will be either gradual or rapid, but nevertheless it will be a change. This particular park, at least up to the present time, has been what I would call a community

park in the sense that people in northern Saskatchewan, and even further south, have used it as a community. There has not been in the past a great influx of tourists from other areas.
What I and the people of Saskatchewan are concerned about is that a corporation is to be given the job of running the park. We would like to know whether the park is still going to serve the community as a community park. What is going to be the cost of accommodation for those who live in the accommodation centres that are to be set up? Will the ordinary people of Saskatchewan be able to afford to use the park as they have until now? Will those who visit the park for a short stay, either with or without camping equipment, be able to obtain the kind of accommodation they need, at reasonable rates? Indeed, will they have access to the park at all? Will the local people, or the expected influx of tourists benefit from the facilities offered by the park?
We are also concerned about the importance of preserving our natural heritage and the beauty of the wilderness there. Not too long ago some young people in Saskatchewan who had recently visited the park wrote me to ask why the cabin of that great naturalist, Grey Owl, which they had assumed was an historic monument, had fallen into decay. I wrote to the department involved and asked what was to be the future of this very important historic monument and I was informed that there were certain plans under way to preserve it.
This is the sort of thing that gives people in northern Saskatchewan cause for concern. They want a place of beauty, a place of natural wilderness, accessible by ordinary means of transportation and which can be enjoyed by ordinary people. I hope that before this debate is over the minister will be able to convince the House that a corporation such as that envisaged will be able to maintain this kind of environment for the people of Saskatchewan. I hope there will be clear guidelines to ensure that the interests and needs of the people of Saskatchewan are looked after. I hope the House will be given the assurance that those who now have accommodation in the park will continue to have that kind of accommodation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want at this time to make a few remarks on the general subject of the importance of parks in our national life. For a long time, of course, during the early period of our
February 10, 1970



development as a nation-this can be said equally of the United States-people looked upon themselves as striving against an overwhelming wilderness which seemingly they might never overcome. However, people of foresight such as President Roosevelt-I refer to Teddy Roosevelt-recognized that wherever man went, he left the land in ruin; that there was a great necessity for setting land apart as a legacy for future generations. In this way they would be in a position to enjoy nature at its best.
In addition, areas of wilderness should be preserved in their virgin state for historic purposes, using the wider sense of the word, so that Canadians both of this and future generations realize what our early settlers and forefathers had to struggle against in opening up this great North American continent. The foresight exhibited by outstanding men such as Teddy Roosevelt has been an invaluable asset to the United States. He was instrumental in setting aside vast stretches of virgin country as the legacy of future generations. The same thing was done in Canada to a considerable extent and we owe a great deal to those men and governments who had the foresight to take this step.
However, this bill, which is an important one, contains provisions with which I disagree. The bill exhibits a trend that is evident in many federal government activities- removing government further and further from the governed. The government is setting up corporations and other faceless organizations to act as a buffer between government, which is elected to be the people's servant, and the people it is supposed to serve. It is my contention that the more directly the government is responsible to the people, the better it functions, because it is then held directly responsible to the people for its activities.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
I note that this bill-and I will not go into this matter at great length now because it can be examined more carefully in committee- changes the description of a number of our national parks. From a quick perusal of the appendices to the bill it would seem that at least four of our parks are to be reduced in size. This reduction may not be significant. The four parks to which I refer are Water ton Lakes, Kootenay, Prince Albert and Prince Edward Island. These may be very minor changes in the boundaries, but this is something we have to find out. In any event, in my judgment this trend is in the wrong direction.
National Parks Act
I notice that the Terra Nova National Park in Newfoundland is to be extended in area under the terms of this bill.
There are many reasons for national parks. The most obvious one, which is perhaps readily recognized by urban people, is for vacation purposes. National parks are places for recreation; that is one of their benefits. Facilities should be provided in suitable terrain set aside for various types of recreation. There are other questions involved. National parks, in my judgment, should be established to preserve in each part of our country typical areas in as near a natural, virgin state as possible in order that people will know what the land was like as God made it.
Some areas of our country have special attractions. In the park that is partly in my own constituency, the Prince Edward Island National Park, there exists one of the finest beaches in Canada. There are excellent beaches in the maritime provinces; in Prince Edward Island, parts of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. More of these beaches should be set aside in the form of parks for public use. In this way everyone, rich or poor, would have access to them and would be able to enjoy their benefits.
Even in Prince Edward Island our beaches are not our only asset. I recommend that a second park be provided in Prince Edward Island. This matter has been under discussion for a long time between the two levels of government. We should set aside additional fine beach areas on the island for national park use. There is also a necessity for setting aside, before it is too late, areas in Prince Edward Island that are as near their virgin state as any to be found, for the preservation of the wildlife which still exists. This would allow the remaining species of wildlife in Prince Edward Island to continue. Perhaps they would not become extinct, as has been the case in respect of too many small animals and birds.
It is too late now to preserve a habitat for many of the small animals that were native to our province. It is not too late to preserve an area which would be a suitable habitat for migratory birds. In Prince Edward Island we have a vast number of migratory birds for which a habitat should be provided in order to preserve their existence. In this way people could enjoy the very relaxing recreation referred to by most people as birdwatching but which I prefer to call communion with nature.

February 10, 1970
National Parks Act
One of the most beneficial experiences that society can have, and which is becoming more and more urbanized, more and more polluted with pollutants and noise, is that of isolation or to be able to go where one can obtain peace, quiet and solitude. I am old-fashioned enough to believe that solitude not only heals the body but heals the mind. It is essential that people experience it periodically if they are to have recreation in the true sense of the word.
Therefore, I recommend strongly that the government consider carefully the provision of not less but more area for national parks, even if these areas cannot be developed at the present time. Land costs will increase and the longer this program is delayed, the harder it will be to accomplish. There will be developments of various kinds, and the environment will be destroyed. It will then be too late to take advantage of these areas. I would urge the minister, if he were here, to consider the necessity of taking action now to protect the future of Canadians yet unborn.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments on Bill C-152, titled "an Act to amend the National Parks Act". I read the bill with interest and taken as a whole, I find it deserves our close attention since it deals with an important subject, that is the expansion and operation of resort areas, the preservation of our wildlife and the development of our natural resources.
I would like to consider the problem mostly from the point of view of Quebec. The previous speaker noted that Quebec may not be a province like the others, that it does not benefit from national parks and that, in comparison with other provinces, its natural resources remain undeveloped.
In that regard, I wish to recall the problem about the famous Forillon Park in the Gaspe Peninsula.
The federal government has been taking steps recently to set up a national park in that area. On the other hand, the Quebec government is also taking steps, having studies made with a view to having a park in the same area which, however, is not intended to be "national". Although it is quite willing to accept the funds required from the federal government.
That is what could be called a constitutional quarrel between the Quebec government

and the federal government. In the meantime, Quebec has yet to have a national park.
Mr. Speaker, it is high time we put an end to our constitutional quarrels, specially when dealing with the development of part of our country, with the development of its natural resources, as in the case of a national park in the Gaspe peninsula which is an underdeveloped area where tourism alone guarantees a certain income, admittedly quite modest, to its people.
On the one hand, the Quebec government tells the people that the government in Ottawa is to blame, that it refuses to negotiate; neither does Ottawa want to negotiate with a view to reaching a reasonable compromise. On the other hand, the federal minister says: We cannot accede fully to the request of the provincial government, because of such and such a section in the constitution, because it could lead to this or that inconvenience, because of such and such a precedent.
Obviously, as a result Quebec has no federal parks. Now, over $335 million were spent in other provinces for national parks, while not a single penny has been spent in Quebec.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
It seems to me that if the provincial government is not reasonable in this particular matter, the federal government for his part, lies low and does not react in any way to the problems and injustices thereby created.
It is high time to wake up and to say, once and for all, that in Quebec as well as in the other provinces, our natural resources must be developed and made profitable, so as to give reasonable impetus to our tourist industry.
It is high time that we should stop playing politics, and passing the buck. Indeed, we have wealth, such as forests, animal life and lakes, but all those things are wasted because no one is concerned about developing them.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. members who spoke before me on the subject were partly right but I do not agree with them when they put the blame for it mainly on the provincial government for his attitude. It is all too easy for the federal government to say that the provincial government is the only one at fault. However, if one gives a close look at the matter, one realizes, that the problem lies on both sides of the fence.
Whenever an interesting bill like Bill C-152 comes up for consideration before the House, there are of course points on which we do not
February 10, 1970

all agree but I dare say that no Canadian will oppose the idea of developing our resources.
I would like to put forward a suggestion and ask the representatives of the federal government responsible for the setting up of the first federal park in Quebec to make some concessions while paying due respect to the wishes of the Quebec government, which they failed to do when the creation of the Forillon park was discussed.
The federal government, allegedly because it is the central government, would like the provinces always to bow down to its wishes. This is a bad attitude and Canadians are still suffering from it.
Last year, I put a question on the order paper. The answer which I received was obviously ridiculous. I asked: Can the minister tell us if discussions have been held between the federal government and the provincial government of Quebec, or if it is intended to hold any? In short, the question read as follows:
Does the government intend to establish other federal parks in the province of Quebec?
The answer was as follows, and I quote:
No.

Then new discussions are begun, following which the ministers answer members' questions arrogantly, stating: We are now considering the possibility of creating a national park.

The weakness of Bill C-152 is that it does not provide lor an alternative that would force the powers that be to get down to work seriously and to find, once and for all, ways and means of developing the country's natural wealth, and in particular Quebec's riches. Clause 1 of the bill provides for the setting up of a Corporation, but is followed by meaningless generalities giving no assurance that the act will actually benefit all Canadians, and not only some of them.

Therefore, when the minister submits the same bill next year, to change at best a few words, if he is asked whether negotiations are underway, tending to make the same advantages available to Quebec as to the other provinces, he will reply that if anything is wrong it is Quebec's fault.

The people of Quebec should at last open their eyes and withdraw their confidence from politicians, those of Quebec as well as those of Ottawa, who have been elected to wage a war of words rather than develop natural resources for the use of Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-152 states that it is an act to amend the National Parks Act. This in itself, I would assume, provides a wide subject for those who wish to speak on it. However, on reading the bill I noticed that there are really only two main points: one is to set up a Crown corporation to administer the national parks, and the other is to designate the boundaries of the national parks which are already established in Canada.
I say at the outset that I take strong exception to the government's plan to set up a Crown corporation to administer our national parks. I think, as do many speakers who preceded me, that this plan will be merely another way of passing the goverment's responsibility to a group of people in a Crown corporation. It will be a way in which the government will endeavour to absolve itself of all responsibility for the operation of national parks.
On looking closely at Bill C-152 we find that should the minister, in his wisdom, feel the Crown corporation is not administering the parks to his liking, he can step in and veto any decision which it makes. I am not sure whether this is an admission by the government that a Crown1 corporation can do a better job of administering our parks. This may be quite true. However, I think it goes much deeper than that, because I believe the government ought not to have the best of two worlds.
I said that I was not in favour of the government setting up a Crown corporation to administer national parks. But in one or two respects this may not be a bad idea, because on looking over the policies of some of our Crown corporations I find that they provide a few benefits over and above those which the government is prepared to provide for the people using our national parks.
I mention in particular the Clear Lake National Park in Manitoba, where a very important and widely publicized golf tournament is held every year. It is called the Grey Owl golf tournament and it opens the season for the national park. This tournament brings great economic benefit to the park at that time of the year. It is held each year during the first week end of June, or thereabouts, and 300 or more entries are received, plus
February 10, 1970

countless hundreds of people who come to enjoy the tournament and to take in the weekend at the park when it is in progress.
On occasion, the sponsors of this golf tournament have approached me to see whether the minister would take into consideration the great contribution that it is mailing at the opening of the season at Clear Lake National Park, and whether certain regulations in relation to the fees normally charged could be altered so that either a subsidy could be granted or at least a special fee set. I understand that this is done in some parts of Canada, but on several occasions when I have approached the minister he has told me this would be impossible.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
To get back to what I said previously, in some respects it may be better for a Crown corporation to take over the administration of the parks, although I would not agree to a full takeover. I would point out that Air Canada, which is a Crown corporation, and Canadian National Railways offer beneficial rates to large parties; they have group fares. But this government will give no consideration to a tournament the size of the Grey Owl golf tournament held in Clear Lake National Park. Green fees last year were raised to $4 and the tournament officials were told, "If you have 300 golfers, you will pay $1,200 for them to play one round apiece." This means $2,400 for the two rounds which they play. In that respect, Mr. Speaker, perhaps a Crown corporation would do a better job than the government is doing. However, I reiterate that I am not in favour of the government turning over all its responsibilities to a Crown corporation.
We all know the many concerns of the people residing in the national parks and of those operating businesses in the parks. In December, 1966, as a result of many protests from residents of the western parks arising from cancellation of long-standing, historic leasing rights by order in council, the Standing Committee on Northern Affairs and National Resources visited Banff and Jasper on a fact-finding mission. During hearings lasting three days the committee found that the citizens affected agreed with the necessity for a change in leasing policy to meet the growing recreational needs of today, while at the same time conforming to the conservation principles of wise management and multiple use of our renewable resources which emerged from the Resources for Tomorrow Conference of 1961.
National Parks Act
The protests arose because the changes were made by administrative decree rather than by act of Parliament, and also because cancellation of perpetual leases provided no compensation in respect of commercial properties. The main protest at that time was supported by a comprehensive brief presen: ed by Mr. G. H. Steer, Q.C., of Edmonton, which argued the illegality of government ac ion by order in council rather than by act of Parliament. But, Mr. Speaker, the committee report tabled in the House completely ignored those representations.
It is no wonder that the leaseholders in many of our parks are at their wits end to know what compensation they can get and what hearing they will receive from a government that arbitrarily passes laws of this nature by order in council. It makes one wonder just what the position of these leaseholders would be if the administration of parks were turned over to a Crown corporation. We all know what has happened in recent times with respect to individuals dealing wiih Crown corporations. I ci e the example of the city of Winnipeg and the people of Manitoba generally and the great difficulty they had when Air Canada decided to move its facilities from Winnipeg to Mon'real. The people concerned in Winnipeg are still looking for answers, mainly because they feel they could not pin the government down since it was a decision by a Crown corporation. The findings of the committee at that lime were another example of the growing tendency of the government to implement policies by administra'ive decree rather than by parliamentary action.
Mr. Speaker, my time is drawing to a close. We in Manitoba have repeatedly requested through the provincial government that the federal government establish a second national park in our province. If one asks representatives of the provincial government, they say that they cannot get an answer from Ottawa. I have approached representatives of the federal government, and they say that Manitoba must make the first move. This creates a very difficult situation for people in all parts of Manitoba.
We in the northern part of the province hoped that the second national park in Manitoba would be situated in an area north of or closely adjacent to the 55th parallel. However, we have been told that studies were made of that area which showed it was not suitable for a national park, and that other areas were being examined. The people living

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my grievance tonight involves the Post Office Department and the Postmaster General and Minister of Communications (Mr. Kierans). I am indeed sorry that the minister has not seen fit to be in the House because I believe he should hear what I have to say. I am disturbed at developments in the Post 

Office Department because I find that little, if any, consideration is being given to any appeal that may come from members of this House, or to representations that come from the people of Canada whom the minister is supposed to serve.
The only product that the Post Office Department has to sell is service, and if it is not intent on rendering that service to the people of Canada it is grossly failing in its responsibilities and obligations to the people of Canada. I believe that practically every member of the House knows and has evidence, in the form of protests, in his files that the Post Office Department is not functioning as well as it used to function. I have been a member of this House for eight years, and I believe that last year I received more complaints about the inefficiency and ineffectiveness of the Post Office than I did in all the previous seven years.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
I am not going to deal with the situation in general tonight, although I was a bit disturbed the other day to receive an urgent letter containing an appeal about the situation in Nigeria which took nine days to come to Ottawa from the city of Toronto. My concern, Mr. Speaker, is with the blanket policy of the Minister of Communications to close all low-income post offices in the country. On May 22, 1969, the Minister of Communications wrote to me stating:
-changing conditions throughout the country, revenue post offices in many of our smaller communities are no longer required. As a consequence, early in 1967 we initiated a program to close these post offices.
In relation to a complaint that I made on June 20, 1969, the Minister of Communications stated in a letter:
In light of our current program to close all small revenue post offices we could not arbitrarily make an exception in this case.
That is the case I was appealing, Mr. Speaker. In other words, the government, through the Minister of Communications, has initiated a policy intended to close all low-income post offices whether or not they are essential to the communities they serve.
The argument the minister uses repeatedly in letters to me when I tried to have him clarify the situation can best be illustrated by saying that he is trying to fit the visitor to the bed. If his legs are too long, he cuts them off; if they are too short, he attempts to stretch them to fit the bed. To be specific, I shall
February 10, 1970

mention a few instances to illustrate that the policy the Minister of Communications has initiated is in many cases completely unjust.
I am not referring to all low-income post offices. I can name at least seven low-income post offices in my constituency that have no justification for continuing. They have very few boxholders and serve very few people, so it is logical that rural route service would be better. But this is not the case in every instance. I want to mention four specific examples. One is the Dickson post office, where there are approximately 30 boxholders in the village and 17 boxholders in the rural area. The cost of this post office is $1,800 a year. The Minister of Communications said it was $2,000 a year, but that is wrong; it is $1,800 a year. The revenue is small, but I maintain that because of the traditional service going back more than 60 years that this post office has rendered, there is no justification for closing it now.
A petition has been signed by every citizen served by this post office, protesting the closing. I am concerned that when I consulted the Minister of Communications, and later investigated the situation on the spot, I learned that in November an official of the post office in Calgary visited the community; he assured the postmaster at Dickson that he had no intention of closing it but was merely investigating the rural route service in the area. However, four weeks later, on December 17, an order was issued to close the post office.
Many of the arguments stated by the Minister of Communications in letters to me are just not logical nor do they actually state the facts. While this is a very small post office, and there is another only a couple of miles away, it will cost far more than $1,800 to provide the service that the people in the village and the area south of the village must have if the post office was closed and rural route delivery substituted. There is no economic gain or saving by closing that post office, and 100 per cent of the people involved want it kept open because it meets their particular needs.
Why is an approach not made to the people to determine whether they want the post office to close or stay open? Why does the government not deal with the matter in a forthright manner and consider the costs of offering a substitute service through the extension of rural route No. 1 from Innisfail? As far as I can determine, this will be much more than the cost of maintaining the post office. No consideration has been given to

maintopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-REFUND OF SALES TAX ON GRAIN STORAGE EQUIPMENT
NATIONAL REVENUE-REFUND OF SALES TAX ON GRAIN STORAGE EQUIPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hoped that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) would be answering my question this evening because I find it easier to get angry with him over the problems we have in western Canada; he should know how to solve our problems; the parliamentary secretary may not. I will try to be logical in my argument in the hope that it might have some influence on the parliamentary secretary.
I received a complaint from a farmer who had built grain storage facilities in Saskatchewan. He has discovered that he cannot get a tax rebate on this building because it is not the right style. I quote from his letter as follows:
-the building we erected was built primarily for grain storage and now holds over 25,000 bushels of wheat. The way the grain situation is now, this could be in there for another 10 years with what other wheat we have on hand and the quotas we are getting, even without seeding another wheat crop.
I ask the parliamentary secretary to note the following:
The provincial government recognized this as a grain storage building and we cannot understand the federal government's view of this.
I quote from another letter received from this person:
We believe that very few people in this economic situation would build a building costing this much to store machinery and let grain sit outside in piles and spoil. When this much more storage space is needed we feel it much wiser to build one large building than 12 to 14 small bins. We already have 17 other granaries varying in size and a 28' x 40' barn lowered and converted into a grain storage bin, all filled to capacity. To add another dozen small bins would be ridiculous.


e (10:10 p.m.)
From the point of view of economics as applied to this farm, it makes more sense to erect one large building for the storage of grain than to buy several grain storage bins. From the answer given me by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cote), or an official of the department, it is not enough, apparently, that a bin should hold grain. It has to look like a grain bin and it should not be capable of use for any purpose but the storage of grain.
I wonder whether the government is serious when it professes to be willing to help farmers who are in trouble because they cannot sell their grain. The Saskatchewan government has recognized that bins of this type are adequate for storage. There is a method by which an individual can apply to his municipality for a permit enabling him to make application for a return of tax. In this case the farmer got a $200 refund, the amount of the 5 per cent sales tax collected by the Saskatchewan government. Thus, one level of government recognizes the principle and I wonder why another level of government declines to do so.
It seems to me the Saskatchewan government acknowledges the seriousness of the situation on the prairies, while the federal government is only playing around. The federal government may not agree with this opinion, but this is what it amounts to. The government should take another look at these cases. Only one farmer has appealed to me, but after talking to other hon. members I know that other farmers are in the same difficulty.
The argument that the grain bins may be used for another purpose is a ridiculous one. No one with any knowledge of the economic situation on the prairies at the present time would believe that a farmer would put up special bins just for the sake of getting a tax rebate. Interest rates alone would rule this out. I maintain that when a farmer puts up a grain storage bin, whether it looks like a granary or not it should be accepted as such provided it holds grain. The Saskatchewan government recognized this principle when it returned the 5 per cent sales tax, and I can see no reason why the federal government should not carry out the intent of its promise to western agriculture in connection with this rebate.
I have one final comment. I am a farmer and if I were erecting another bin on my farm I would probably choose a quonset type

of construction because it would make the best sense. If I were to follow the government's logic I would be dissuaded from doing so. The situation to which I have drawn attention occurs frequently on the prairies. These farmers have a case in equity, and it should be considered.
